novenas.note: The promises said to have been made to Saint Bridget for seven Hail Marys a day are a tradition, not a guarantee.

novenas.name: Novena to Our Lady of the Rosary
novenas.about: A Rosary each day for nine days before the feast of 7 October.
novenas.when: 28 September to 6 October.

novenas.name: The fifty-four day Rosary novena
novenas.about: Six novenas of the Rosary in a row: three in petition and three in thanksgiving, whether or not the request seems answered.
novenas.when: Any time. Days 1 to 27 in petition, days 28 to 54 in thanksgiving. The mysteries are usually taken in turn (joyful, sorrowful, glorious; the luminous may be added).
novenas.note: Twenty-seven days in petition, then twenty-seven in thanksgiving, whatever the answer seems to be. A missed day does not undo it, and a shorter novena is just as good.
conditions: Pray five decades of the Rosary each day for fifty-four days, for one intention.
For the first twenty-seven days, ask.
For the last twenty-seven days, give thanks, trusting that God has heard.

novenas.name: The Novena of Grace (Saint Francis Xavier)
novenas.about: The Jesuits’ novena to Saint Francis Xavier, which asks above all for a holy life and death, and then for the reader’s request, but only if it is for God’s glory and the good of the soul.
novenas.when: 4 to 12 March, ending on 12 March, the day he and Saint Ignatius were canonized (1622). It is also made from 25 November to 3 December, before his feast, and at any time.

novenas.name: Novena for the holy souls
novenas.about: Nine days of prayer for the dead, at any time or from 24 October to 1 November.
novenas.when: 24 October to 1 November, ending on the eve of All Souls. Any time of year, especially after a death.

novenas.name: Christmas anticipation
novenas.about: The Saint Andrew prayer, said from 30 November until Christmas Eve, traditionally fifteen times a day.
novenas.when: 30 November (Saint Andrew) to 24 December: 25 days, so not strictly a novena. The Church’s own Christmas novena is 16 (or 17) to 24 December.
novenas.note: Fifteen times a day is a custom. Once a day, said with attention, is enough.

novenas.name: Novena to Saint Gerard Majella
novenas.about: Nine days with the Redemptorist lay brother whom mothers, expectant mothers and those hoping for a child ask for help.
novenas.when: 7 to 15 October.
novenas.note: Pray too for those who long for children and do not have them.

novenas.name: Novena to Saint Dymphna
novenas.about: Nine days with the virgin martyr venerated at Geel, patron of those who suffer in mind and nerves and of those who care for them.
novenas.when: 6 to 14 May.
novenas.note: Her story is a medieval legend. Prayer for those who suffer in mind goes with good care, never instead of it.

novenas.name: Novena to Saint Benedict
novenas.about: Nine days with the father of Western monks, who asked his sons to prefer nothing to the love of Christ.
novenas.when: 2 to 10 July, before his feast of 11 July. Monks also keep 21 March, the traditional day of his death (12 to 20 March).
novenas.note: The Saint Benedict medal is a sacramental, not an amulet; its letters are prayers.

novenas.name: Novena to Saint Patrick
novenas.about: Nine days with the apostle of Ireland.
novenas.when: 8 to 16 March.

novenas.name: Novena to Saint Raphael the Archangel
novenas.about: Nine days with the angel who guided Tobias: for travellers, for the sick, and for those looking for a good husband or wife.
novenas.when: 20 to 28 September, before the feast of the three archangels; or 15 to 23 October, before his former feast of 24 October.

novenas.name: The Nine First Fridays
novenas.about: Holy Communion received on the first Friday of nine months in a row, in honour of the Sacred Heart and in reparation for sin. It comes from the revelations reported by Saint Margaret Mary Alacoque at Paray-le-Monial from 1673; the promise for nine First Fridays is in a letter of hers of 1688. The Church warmly recommends devotion to the Heart of Jesus; this is one long-loved way of living it.
conditions: Receive Holy Communion on the first Friday of the month, at Mass if you can.
Receive it in a state of grace: if you are aware of serious sin, go to confession first; confession is not a separate condition in the saint’s own account, though many guides add it.
Offer the Communion in honour of the Sacred Heart and in reparation for sin, your own and the world’s.
Keep this on nine first Fridays in a row.
Many also spend time before the Blessed Sacrament on the Thursday evening or the Friday, as Saint Margaret Mary was asked to; this is a counsel, not a condition.
novenas.note: Saint Margaret Mary reported a promise of the grace of final repentance to those who keep the nine. The Church recommends the devotion, but a private revelation adds nothing to the faith, and the promise is no guarantee apart from faith, love and repentance. If a month is missed, those who keep it as she reported begin the nine again; missing one is not a sin, and every Communion made with love is worth making.

novenas.name: The Five First Saturdays
novenas.about: Five first Saturdays in a row kept in reparation to the Immaculate Heart of Mary: confession, Communion, five decades of the Rosary, and a quarter of an hour keeping Our Lady company with its mysteries. Sister Lúcia of Fatima reported that Our Lady asked for it at Pontevedra in Spain on 10 December 1925. The Bishop of Leiria-Fatima approved the devotion in 1939.

perDay.title: Her Immaculate Conception
perDay.text: Lúcia gave five reasons for the five Saturdays, five kinds of offence against Our Lady. Many give one Saturday to each. The first: thank God for preserving her from all sin, and make amends for those who deny it.

perDay.title: Her virginity
perDay.text: Thank God for Mary’s lasting virginity, wholly given to him, and make amends for those who scorn it.

perDay.title: Her divine motherhood
perDay.text: Thank God that she is Mother of God and our mother, and make amends for those who refuse to receive her as their mother.

perDay.title: For children
perDay.text: Pray for children, and make amends for those who teach them indifference, contempt or hatred towards their Mother.

perDay.title: Her images
perDay.text: Make amends for those who insult her images, and ask for a heart that honours what it loves.

conditions: Go to confession with the intention of making reparation to the Immaculate Heart of Mary. It need not be on the Saturday; it is commonly allowed within about eight days before or after, provided you are in a state of grace when you receive Communion.
Receive Holy Communion on the first Saturday with the same intention; Communion at a Saturday evening Mass is commonly accepted.
Pray five decades of the Rosary.
Keep Our Lady company for fifteen minutes, meditating on one or more mysteries of the Rosary; this is in addition to the five decades.
Offer all of it in reparation to the Immaculate Heart, on five first Saturdays in a row.
If you forgot to make the intention at confession, it can be made at your next confession.
novenas.note: Sister Lúcia reported Our Lady’s promise to help at the hour of death those who keep the five. Like every private revelation it may be accepted freely, and it does not work apart from love and conversion. The request is for five months in a row; if one is missed, begin again, without anxiety. If Saturday is impossible for a just reason, ask a priest whether the following Sunday may serve.

novenas.name: The Thirteen Tuesdays of Saint Anthony
novenas.about: Thirteen Tuesdays in a row given to Saint Anthony of Padua, most often the thirteen before his feast on 13 June. Tradition ties Tuesday to him because he was buried on a Tuesday, and thirteen recalls the date of his death and feast.
conditions: On each Tuesday, pray to God with Saint Anthony’s help; many go to Mass and receive Communion that day.
Add a prayer in his honour, and perhaps a few lines of the Gospel; he was a preacher and is a Doctor of the Church.
Many add an alms for the poor, the old custom of Saint Anthony’s bread.
novenas.note: The Church attaches no promise to the thirteen Tuesdays; leaflets that promise a favour to anyone who completes them go beyond her teaching. If a Tuesday is missed, simply carry on.

novenas.name: The Seven Sundays of Saint Joseph
novenas.about: Seven Sundays in a row given to Saint Joseph, traditionally the seven before his feast on 19 March, praying each Sunday the prayer of his seven sorrows and joys. Each sorrow and joy is a moment from the Gospels of the childhood of Jesus, where Joseph’s trouble is turned to gladness.

perDay.title: The angel’s message
perDay.text: Joseph’s distress at the thought of sending Mary away, and his joy when the angel tells him of the Incarnation.

perDay.title: The birth in poverty
perDay.text: His grief at the poverty of the birth, and his joy at the angels’ song.

perDay.title: The Circumcision
perDay.text: The first blood of the Child, and the joy of the name Jesus.

perDay.title: Simeon’s prophecy
perDay.text: The sword foretold for Jesus and Mary, and the salvation of many foretold with it.

perDay.title: The flight into Egypt
perDay.text: The hardship of exile, and the joy of having God always with him.

perDay.title: The return to Nazareth
perDay.text: His fear of Archelaus, and the peace of the home at Nazareth.

perDay.title: The finding in the Temple
perDay.text: Three days of searching for the lost Child, and the joy of finding him.

conditions: On each of the seven Sundays, pray the Seven Sorrows and Joys of Saint Joseph, with an Our Father, Hail Mary and Glory Be after each.
Many receive Holy Communion on these Sundays in his honour, which Sunday Mass makes simple.
A gentle way to keep it: pray the whole prayer each Sunday, and stay longest with one sorrow and joy, in order, with its Gospel passage.
novenas.note: The Church attaches no promise to the seven Sundays. If one is missed, carry on; the devotion can also be kept at any time of the year.

novenas.name: The Fifteen Saturdays of the Rosary
novenas.about: Fifteen Saturdays in a row honouring the fifteen traditional mysteries of the Rosary, one mystery each Saturday. It grew up around the Confraternity of the Rosary, which once had indulgences for it.

perDay.title: The Annunciation
perDay.text: Joyful mysteries.

perDay.title: The Agony in the Garden
perDay.text: Sorrowful mysteries.

perDay.title: The Resurrection
perDay.text: Glorious mysteries.

perDay.title: The Descent of the Holy Spirit

conditions: On each Saturday, pray five decades of the Rosary.
Spend some quiet time with one mystery, taking the fifteen traditional mysteries in order.
Confession and Communion on some of the Saturdays were once asked of Confraternity members for the indulgence; today they are a good counsel, not a condition.
novenas.note: No promise is attached. Carry on if a Saturday is missed.

novenas.name: Thirty Days’ Prayer to Saint Joseph
novenas.about: A long prayer to Saint Joseph said each day for thirty days for one intention, recalling his sorrows and joys from Nazareth to Egypt and back. It was printed in American prayer books of the 1890s.
novenas.note: No promise is attached by the Church. If a day is missed, carry on the next.

novenas.name: Consecration to Jesus through Mary
novenas.about: Saint Louis de Montfort’s gift of oneself to Jesus Christ through Mary, made after a preparation of thirty-three days: twelve days of turning away from the spirit of the world, then a week each on knowledge of oneself, of Mary and of Jesus Christ. He sets it out in his True Devotion to the Blessed Virgin; it is renewed each year.
novenas.when: Thirty-three days ending on the eve of a feast of Our Lady, the consecration made on the feast. The Immaculate Conception (begin 5 November) is shown here; to end on another feast, such as the Annunciation, the Assumption or Our Lady of the Rosary, choose “Another day” and begin thirty-three days before its eve.

perDay.text: Ask for freedom from what in you is set against the Gospel: vanity, love of comfort, fear of others’ opinion.

perDay.text: Ask to know Christ, the Wisdom of God made man, and to love him more. Tomorrow is the day of the consecration: go to confession, receive Holy Communion with the intention of giving yourself to Jesus through Mary, and after Communion make the act of consecration. Montfort suggests a small gift as well: a fast, an alms or an act of self-denial.

conditions: Twelve days of prayer about leaving behind the spirit of the world.
First week: ask for knowledge of yourself and sorrow for your sins.
Second week: ask for knowledge of the Blessed Virgin.
Third week: ask for knowledge of Jesus Christ.
At the end: go to confession and Holy Communion with the intention of giving yourself to Jesus through Mary; after Communion say the act of consecration, and sign a written copy that day.
Montfort suggests offering some small gift that day, such as a fast, an alms or an act of self-denial.
Renew the consecration each year on the same date; it may be renewed briefly every day.
novenas.note: Montfort gives no rule about missed days: carry on. The aim is a free and loving gift of yourself, not an examination. His own act of consecration is long; until it can be given here from a sure text, “My Queen, my Mother” is offered for the day itself.

novenas.name: Novena to Our Lady
novenas.about: Nine days of asking Our Lady’s help with one intention.

novenas.name: Rosary novena
novenas.about: The Rosary each day for nine days, for one intention.

novenas.name: A novena of your own
novenas.about: Choose the prayers and the number of days yourself.

intro: Begin by asking the Holy Spirit for light: to see your life as God sees it, with truth and with mercy.
These questions are prompts, not a test. Pass over what does not apply. If you are unsure whether something was a sin, or how serious it was, say so simply to the priest and let him help you.
Mortal sins, those of grave matter done with full knowledge and deliberate consent, are to be confessed by kind and, as far as you can, by number.
If you are troubled by scruples, keep to a few questions, follow your confessor’s advice, and do not confess again what has already been forgiven.

sections.title: I am the Lord your God: you shall not have strange gods before me
questions: Have I given God time each day in prayer, or left him out of my days?
Have I doubted or denied what the Church teaches, or neglected to learn my faith?
Have I put my trust in superstition, horoscopes, fortune-telling or the occult?
Have I despaired of God’s mercy, or presumed on it while planning to sin?
Have I let money, work, comfort, a person or my own reputation take the first place that belongs to God?
Have I received Holy Communion while conscious of grave sin, or concealed a grave sin in confession?

sections.title: You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain
questions: Have I used the name of God, of Jesus, of Our Lady or the saints carelessly or in anger?
Have I cursed anyone, or wished evil on them?
Have I sworn a false oath, or broken a vow or a serious promise made before God?
Have I spoken with contempt of God, the Church or holy things?

sections.title: Remember to keep holy the Lord’s day
questions: Have I missed Mass on a Sunday or holy day of obligation through my own fault?
Have I come late or left early without need, or been wilfully inattentive?
Have I done or required unnecessary work on Sunday that kept me or others from worship and rest?
Have I kept the days of fasting and abstinence, and the fast before Communion?
Have I gone to confession at least once in the year, and received Communion in the Easter season?
Have I contributed to the support of the Church according to my means?

sections.title: Honour your father and your mother
questions: Have I honoured and cared for my parents, especially in their need or old age?
Have I neglected my duties to my spouse: to love, to be faithful in small things, to pray together?
Have I neglected my children: their faith, their formation, my time and attention?
Have I given bad example at home by my anger, my words or my habits?
Have I shown proper respect to those in lawful authority, and treated justly those under mine?

sections.title: You shall not kill
questions: Have I harmed anyone physically, or wished to?
Have I had, advised, paid for or helped with an abortion?
Have I harboured hatred, nursed resentment, or refused to forgive?
Have I given way to anger, insults, contempt or cruelty in word or act?
Have I harmed my own body by drunkenness, drugs, gluttony or reckless risk?
Have I led another person into sin by my words, example or encouragement?
Have I ignored someone in real need whom I could have helped?

sections.title: You shall not commit adultery. You shall not covet your neighbour’s wife
questions: Have I been unfaithful to my spouse in act or in deliberate desire?
Have I engaged in sexual acts outside marriage, alone or with another?
Have I looked at pornography, or sought out impure images, shows, books or conversation?
Have I wilfully entertained impure thoughts or desires?
Have I used contraception, or closed the marital act to life by sterilisation?
Have I treated another person as an object, by my eyes, my speech or my conduct?
Have I been immodest in dress or behaviour, or put myself in occasions of sin I could have avoided?

sections.title: You shall not steal. You shall not covet your neighbour’s goods
questions: Have I stolen, kept what was not mine, or damaged another’s property? Have I made it good?
Have I cheated, defrauded, or been dishonest in business, taxes or expenses?
Have I failed to give an honest day’s work, or to pay a just wage and my debts on time?
Have I wasted money, gambled irresponsibly, or lived beyond what is right for my state?
Have I been greedy or envious of what others have?
Have I given to the poor and to those in need, in proportion to what I have been given?

sections.title: You shall not bear false witness against your neighbour
questions: Have I lied, or deceived others by half-truths or silence?
Have I damaged someone’s good name by telling lies about them?
Have I revealed the real faults of others without good reason, or enjoyed gossip?
Have I judged others rashly, assuming the worst without grounds?
Have I betrayed a confidence, or failed to keep a secret I was bound to keep?
Have I failed to speak up for the truth, or for a person, when I should have?

sections.title: The roots of sin
questions: Pride: do I need to be noticed, to be right, to have the last word? Do I refuse correction?
Envy: am I saddened by another’s good, or pleased at their failure?
Sloth: do I put off prayer and duty? Do I waste hours on screens and distraction?
Anger: am I impatient, sharp, hard to live with?
Gluttony: do I eat or drink past what is good for me? Is there anything I cannot do without?
Have I been ungrateful for what God has given me?
What is the one fault that does most harm to those I live with?

steps.title: Before you go
steps.text: Ask the Holy Spirit for light, examine your conscience, and be sorry. Sorrow is an act of the will more than a feeling: you turn away from the sin and intend, with God’s help, not to commit it again.

steps.title: Begin
steps.text: Make the Sign of the Cross. The priest may greet you or read a few words of Scripture. Then say: “Bless me, Father, for I have sinned. It has been (how long) since my last confession.”

steps.title: Confess your sins
steps.text: Say them plainly and briefly. Grave sins are confessed by kind and, as far as you remember, by number. There is no need for the story around them. When you have finished, say: “For these and all the sins of my past life, I am sorry.”

steps.title: Listen
steps.text: The priest may offer a word of counsel. He will give you a penance: a prayer or an act to do afterwards. If you do not understand it or cannot do it, say so.

steps.title: Make an act of contrition
steps.text: Say an act of contrition aloud. Any sincere form will do; the traditional one is below.

steps.title: Receive absolution
steps.text: The priest extends his hand and says the words of absolution. Make the Sign of the Cross as he blesses you, and answer “Amen”. If he says, “Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good”, answer, “His mercy endures for ever.”

steps.title: Afterwards
steps.text: Do your penance as soon as you can, and give thanks. Then let it go: what has been absolved is forgiven.

examen.about: A few quiet minutes at the end of the day, looking back over it with God. The pattern is that of Saint Ignatius of Loyola.

steps.title: Become aware of God’s presence
steps.text: Be still for a moment. God has been with you through every hour of this day and is with you now. Ask him for light to see the day as he sees it.

steps.title: Give thanks
steps.text: Walk back through the day and notice what you were given: a person, a conversation, a meal, a moment of beauty, a task finished, a difficulty you were carried through. Thank him for each.

steps.title: Look over the day
steps.text: Go through the day hour by hour. Where did you feel drawn towards God, more alive, more able to love? Where did you pull away, or act from fear, irritation or self-seeking? Notice without excusing yourself and without beating yourself up.

steps.title: Ask for forgiveness
steps.text: Choose the one moment that most needs it and speak to the Lord about it honestly. Tell him you are sorry, and receive his mercy.

steps.title: Look to tomorrow
steps.text: What is coming tomorrow? Where will you most need his help? Ask for it now, in particular. Then entrust the night to him.

lectio.about: Lectio Divina is the Church’s ancient way of praying with Scripture: reading slowly enough that the reading becomes a conversation.

steps.title: Read
steps.text: Read the passage slowly, aloud if you can. Then read it again. Do not study it yet. Notice the word or phrase that catches you.

steps.title: Reflect
steps.text: Stay with that word or phrase. Turn it over. Why this one, today? What in your life does it touch?

steps.title: Respond
steps.text: Speak to God about what you have heard, in your own words: thanks, sorrow, a question, a request. If it helps, write it down.

steps.title: Rest
steps.text: Now say nothing. Simply remain with him. When your mind wanders, return gently, with the word you were given.

guides.title: Mental prayer
guides.sub: A quarter of an hour of silent prayer
guides.about: Mental prayer is simply time spent alone with God: a little reading to give the mind something to hold, and then a conversation. The saints call it the one practice that changes everything else. Fifteen minutes is enough to begin with; the same time each day matters more than the length.

steps.title: Come into his presence
steps.text: Be still. God is here, and he sees you. Make an act of faith in his presence and ask him to teach you to pray.

steps.title: Read
steps.text: Read the passage slowly. You are not studying it. You are listening for what the Lord wants to say to you in it today.

steps.title: Consider
steps.text: Stay with one thing that struck you: a word of Christ, something he did, the way someone answered him. What does it show you about him? What does it ask of you?

steps.title: Speak to him
steps.text: Now talk with him about it in your own words, as one friend to another. Tell him what you love, what you fear, what you want. Listen as well as speak. If you grow dry or distracted, go back to the passage for a moment.

steps.title: Resolve
steps.text: Choose one small, definite thing to do today because of this prayer. Small enough that you will really do it.

steps.title: Give thanks
steps.text: Thank him for this time, ask pardon for your distractions, and entrust the day to Our Lady.

guides.title: A visit to the Blessed Sacrament
guides.sub: A few minutes before the tabernacle
guides.about: Christ is truly present in the tabernacle of every Catholic church, and he waits there to be visited. A visit need not be long. These steps are a guide for the first few times; after that, do as love suggests.

steps.title: Adore
steps.text: Genuflect, and kneel if you can. He is here: the same Jesus who was born at Bethlehem and rose from the tomb. Tell him you believe it.

steps.title: Thank
steps.text: Thank him for coming to you in Holy Communion, for staying in this place, and for whatever today has brought.

steps.title: Ask pardon
steps.text: Tell him simply where you have failed him since you last came, and ask his mercy.

steps.title: Ask
steps.text: Bring him the people and the needs you are carrying. Name them one by one.

steps.title: Receive him in desire
steps.text: Ask him to come into your heart now, as he would in Communion.

steps.title: Stay
steps.text: Before you go, be silent for a moment and simply look at him. Then make the Sign of the Cross and take him with you.

guides.title: Thanksgiving after Communion
guides.about: For a few minutes after Holy Communion, Christ is as close to you as he will ever be on earth. The Church has always urged the faithful not to hurry away. Stay after Mass if you can, or use the silence after Communion.

steps.title: Be still
steps.text: He is within you. Say nothing for a moment. Let him be welcome.

steps.title: Adore
steps.text: Make an act of faith and love in your own words, or with these.

steps.title: Thank
steps.text: Thank him for this Communion and for the graces of your whole life: your baptism, your faith, the people who brought you to him.

steps.title: Ask
steps.text: Ask now, while he is with you, for what you most need, and for those you love.

steps.title: Offer
steps.text: Give him the day or the week ahead, and yourself with it.

guides.title: Offering the day
guides.sub: Two minutes at the start of the day
guides.about: Saint Francis de Sales gives four short steps for the morning: thank and adore; offer the day; look ahead at what it holds and how you will meet it; and ask for help. It takes two minutes, before the day takes hold of you.

steps.title: Thank and adore
steps.text: Before anything else, turn to God. Thank him for the night and for this new day, and adore him who made you and keeps you in being.

steps.title: Offer the day
steps.text: This day is given to you to spend well, for eternity. Give it to him now: your work, your joys, your troubles, the people you will meet.

steps.title: Look ahead
steps.text: Think through what today will bring: the work, the people, the places where you are likely to fail. Choose now how you will meet one of them, in particular.

steps.title: Ask for help
steps.text: You can do none of this alone. Ask for the grace you will need, and put yourself in the care of Our Lady and of your guardian angel.

guides.title: A monthly recollection
guides.sub: An hour apart, once a month
guides.about: Many saints kept a regular time apart to look at their lives before God; Saint John Bosco taught his boys a monthly exercise of this kind. An hour is enough: in a church, on a walk or in a quiet room. Go slowly. This is for growth, not for self-reproach.

steps.title: Come apart
steps.text: “Come apart into a desert place, and rest a little” (Mark 6:31). Leave everything else aside for this hour. Put yourself in God’s presence and ask the Holy Spirit for light.

steps.title: Look back over the month
steps.text: Go back over the month, week by week. What were you given? Where did you see God at work? What went badly, and why?

steps.title: Your rule of life
steps.text: Look at what you try to do each day and each week. Is it too much, or too little? Is there one thing to drop, or one to add? Change one thing at most.

steps.title: One thing to work on
steps.text: Choose the one fault that most often gets in the way of love, and one small way to work against it this month. Be patient with yourself: virtues grow slowly, and God is patient with you.

steps.title: Confession
steps.text: If you can, go to confession this week. If you have not yet decided when, decide now.

steps.title: The end of life
steps.text: The saints advise thinking now and then of the end of life: not so as to be afraid, but so as to live today as you would wish to be found. Ask for the grace of a good death. If this is too close to a grief or an illness of your own, pass over it today.

steps.title: Resolve and offer
steps.text: Write down what you resolve for this month, and give it, and yourself, to God.

guides.title: A yearly review
guides.sub: Once a year, the heart looked over and set right
guides.about: Saint Francis de Sales asks that once a year the soul be examined and renewed, as a clock is taken apart and cleaned. The new year, your birthday, the anniversary of your baptism or the start of Advent are good times. Allow an hour or more.

steps.title: Thanks for the year
steps.text: Go back over the year, season by season, and thank God for what it held: people, graces, joys, even the trials you were carried through.

steps.title: Your prayer
steps.text: How has your prayer been this year? What helped, and what got in the way? Where did you meet God most?

steps.title: The sacraments
steps.text: Mass, Communion, confession: how often, and how? Is there one thing to change?

steps.title: Your duties
steps.text: Your family, your work or studies, your health: where have you been faithful, and where not? Be honest, and gentle.

steps.title: Charity
steps.text: The poor, the lonely, those hard to love: what have you done for Christ in them this year, and what could you do?

steps.title: Your rule for the year ahead
steps.text: Choose again what you will try to do each day, each week and each month. Keep it small enough to keep.

steps.title: Renew your baptism
steps.text: Renew the promises of your baptism: reject sin, and Satan and all his works and empty promises; then say the Creed slowly, and give yourself to God again.

guides.title: Night prayer
guides.sub: Compline: the Church’s prayer before sleep
guides.about: Since the time of Saint Benedict the Church has ended the day with Compline, the last of the hours of prayer. This is a short form of it, made from its oldest parts: a call for help, a look back over the day, a night psalm, a short reading, the Song of Simeon and Our Lady’s antiphon. Say it slowly, at the very end of the day, and then go to sleep in peace.

steps.title: Begin
steps.text: Make the Sign of the Cross. Ask, in the old words of this hour, for a quiet night and a perfect end, which means a good death when it comes. Then call on God for help.

steps.title: Look back
steps.text: Be still for a minute and look back over the day with God. Thank him for one thing he gave you. Then see where you failed to love, and say so simply. Do not dwell on it: you are about to give it all to his mercy.

steps.title: A psalm for the night
steps.text: Psalm 4 has been said at this hour since the time of Saint Benedict. Read it slowly. Its last lines are the prayer of anyone lying down to sleep: “In peace in the self same I will sleep, and I will rest.”

steps.title: A word for the night
steps.text: For centuries these words of Saint Peter opened Compline. Hear them, and then give yourself into God’s hands with the words Christ said on the Cross.

steps.title: The Song of Simeon
steps.text: Old Simeon took the child Jesus in his arms and was ready to go in peace. Say his song as your own at the close of the day.

steps.title: Ask his protection
steps.text: Ask God to guard this house and everyone in it through the night, and receive his blessing.

steps.title: Our Lady
steps.text: End the day, as the Church does, with Mary. Then go to sleep without more words.

guides.title: A midday pause
guides.sub: Two or three minutes in the middle of the day
guides.about: The Church has always prayed at midday. The psalmist spoke to God “evening and morning, and at noon”, and Saint Peter went up on the housetop to pray about the sixth hour. This pause is short: stop what you are doing, remember God, look at how the morning has gone, and begin the afternoon again with him.

steps.title: Stop
steps.text: Put down what you are doing and take a breath. God is here, in this place and in the middle of this day, as truly as in church.

steps.title: The morning
steps.text: Look back over the morning quickly and without judging: what went well, what did not, where you remembered God and where you forgot him. Thank him, and ask pardon in a word.

steps.title: Your focus
steps.text: Look at the habit you are working on. How has it gone this morning? Do not count or grade it. Ask for help with it this afternoon, in one particular place.

steps.title: Offer the afternoon
steps.text: Give him the rest of the day: the work, the people, whatever is waiting. Then say the Angelus, which the Church prays at noon.

guides.title: Praying a prayer slowly
guides.about: Saint Ignatius of Loyola calls this the second method of prayer. You take a prayer you know by heart, the Our Father or another, and stay with each word for as long as it gives you something before going on. It is the opposite of saying prayers quickly. Saint Francis de Sales says that one Our Father said devoutly is worth more than many prayers hurried over.

steps.title: Settle
steps.text: Kneel or sit, whichever helps you more, and keep your eyes closed or resting on one place. Remember whom you are about to speak to. You need not reach the end of the prayer: a single word may be enough for today. If you stopped partway last time, say the words you have already prayed, and begin where you left off.

steps.title: Ask, and finish
steps.text: When your time is over, turn in a few words to the one you have been praying to, and ask for the grace or virtue you most need. Then say the rest of the prayer through in the ordinary way, and give thanks.

guides.title: Before Mass
guides.about: Saint Francis de Sales advises beginning Mass by placing yourself in God’s presence, confessing your unworthiness and asking pardon. These steps can be made at home before you leave, or in the pew before Mass begins. A few minutes are enough; what matters is that you come knowing what you are coming to.

steps.title: Be recollected
steps.text: At Mass the sacrifice of Christ on the Cross is made present, and you are going to take part in it. Put aside the hurry that brought you here, and be still. Remember whose house you are entering.

steps.title: Read the Gospel
steps.text: Read the Gospel of the day slowly, so that when it is proclaimed you will already know it. Notice one word or phrase to carry with you through the Mass.

steps.title: What you bring
steps.text: Bring the people and the needs you are carrying, and name them. When the gifts are brought to the altar, you can place them there in spirit, and yourself with them.

steps.title: Look at your conscience
steps.text: Look briefly at your conscience and be sorry for your faults; for everyday faults, sincere sorrow is enough. If you are aware of a grave sin, go to confession before you receive Communion: you are still welcome at Mass, and you can make a spiritual communion today. If you are unsure, ask a priest, and do not torment yourself.

steps.title: The fast
steps.text: Before Communion, fast for an hour from food and drink. Water and medicine do not break the fast, and the elderly, the sick and those who care for them are excused. If you have broken it by mistake, do not receive at this Mass: you may receive at a later Mass once the hour has passed, or make a spiritual communion today, with a quiet heart. It is not a sin to have forgotten.

steps.title: A prayer before Mass
steps.text: Say this old prayer slowly. It names the four ends for which the Mass is offered: to adore God, to thank him, to make reparation for sin, and to ask for what we need.

steps.title: Offer yourself
steps.text: Saint Francis de Sales asks you to offer the sacrifice to the Father together with the priest and all the people. Offer yourself with it: your week, your work, your troubles, your body and soul.

guides.title: Forgiving someone
guides.about: Christ asks us to forgive, and taught us to ask for it every day in the Our Father. Forgiveness is not a feeling. The Catechism says plainly that “it is not in our power not to feel or to forget an offense”; what is in our power is to give the hurt to God and to ask good for the one who caused it. This may take many prayers, and it need not be done all at once; go as far as you can today. If you have been abused or are in danger, getting safe and telling someone come first: forgiving never means keeping silent or staying in harm’s way.

steps.title: Come to Christ
steps.text: Come before Christ as you are, perhaps still angry or sore. He was betrayed by a friend, deserted by others and mocked as he died, and he prayed for those who crucified him. He understands this from the inside.

steps.title: Name the hurt
steps.text: Tell him honestly what was done and what it has cost you. Do not make it smaller than it was, or larger. Forgiveness begins with the truth, not with pretending nothing happened.

steps.title: What forgiving is
steps.text: To forgive is to give up the wish for revenge and to hand the debt over to God. It does not mean saying that the wrong was right, trusting again at once, or staying where you are in danger. Reconciliation needs both people; forgiveness needs only you and God’s grace.

steps.title: The parable
steps.text: Read the parable of the servant who was forgiven a vast debt and would not forgive a small one. We forgive because we have been forgiven far more.

steps.title: Leave justice to God
steps.text: If wrong was done, it matters, and God does not overlook it. Give the judgement to him. When Christ was reviled he did not revile, and when he suffered he did not threaten; on the Cross he commended himself into his Father’s hands. You may still seek justice in the right way; what you lay down is revenge.

steps.title: Pray for them by name
steps.text: Say the person’s name before God and ask one good thing for them: that they may know God, or be healed, or find peace. If you can only say the words, say them; the will is enough, and the feelings may come later.

steps.title: Our Father
steps.text: Pray the Our Father slowly, and pause at “as we forgive those who trespass against us”. If the hurt returns tomorrow, forgive again: Christ said seventy times seven.

guides.title: Offering a suffering
guides.sub: Joining what hurts to the Cross of Christ
guides.about: Saint Paul rejoiced in his sufferings, because in his flesh he filled up “those things that are wanting of the sufferings of Christ” for the Church. Christ’s sufferings lack nothing in themselves; but he lets us share in his work, so that what we suffer in union with him can help others. Saint John Paul II wrote a whole letter on this, Salvifici Doloris (1984). Offering a suffering is not pretending that it does not hurt, nor refusing relief: it is giving God what you are actually carrying.

steps.title: Say what it is
steps.text: Tell God plainly what you are suffering: pain, illness, worry, loss, a hard situation that will not change. He does not ask you to call it light. Christ himself prayed that the chalice might pass from him.

steps.title: Take the help there is
steps.text: Use the treatment, rest and pain relief you need, and let others help you. That is not a lack of faith or of courage. What you offer is what remains when you have done what you reasonably can.

steps.title: Look at the Cross
steps.text: Look at Christ crucified, or picture him. He did not explain suffering away; he entered it and filled it with his love. Read Saint Paul’s words slowly.

steps.title: Join it to his
steps.text: Tell him that you join what you are suffering to his sufferings, and ask him to use it. Saint John Henry Newman wrote: “If I am in sickness, my sickness may serve him; in perplexity, my perplexity may serve him; if I am in sorrow, my sorrow may serve him.”

steps.title: For someone
steps.text: Choose someone to offer it for: a person who is struggling, someone far from God, someone who has died, the Church. Name them.

steps.title: Offer it
steps.text: Make the offering in these words or your own. Then leave it with him; you need not renew it every minute. Once given, it stays given.

guides.title: Before a decision
guides.sub: Saint Ignatius on making a good choice
guides.about: Saint Ignatius of Loyola gives careful advice for choosing before God when there is a real choice between things that are good or allowed. It is not for deciding whether to do something wrong, and it is not for re-deciding a vocation already given for life, such as a marriage or the priesthood. These are his steps for a quiet time, when you can think clearly. Take your time, over one sitting or several, and for a serious decision talk it over with a wise person or your confessor as well.

steps.title: Ask for light
steps.text: Ask the Holy Spirit for light. Tell God that you want to choose what is best for his glory and your salvation, whatever it costs, and ask him to move your will.

steps.title: Not in desolation
steps.text: If you are in a time of desolation, dark, anxious or discouraged, do not make a change now. Saint Ignatius’s rule is to stand firm, in desolation, in the resolutions you made before it, and to decide when you are at peace.

steps.title: Freedom first
steps.text: Before weighing anything, look at your own heart. Ignatius asks you to be “as in the middle of a balance”, not leaning either way before you have seen the reasons. If you cannot yet be free, ask for the grace to want only what God wants.

steps.title: For and against
steps.text: Write down, plainly and honestly, the advantages and the dangers of each way. Then look where reason more inclines, not where your fears or desires pull you.

steps.title: Advise a stranger
steps.text: Imagine someone you have never met, whom you wish every good, coming to you with this same choice. What would you tell them to do, for God’s glory and their good? Give yourself the same advice.

steps.title: From the end
steps.text: Picture yourself at the point of death, and then before God at the judgement. Looking back from there, which way would you want to have chosen? Choose that way now.

steps.title: Offer the choice
steps.text: When you have chosen, offer the decision to God and ask him to receive and confirm it. Notice, as you live with it, whether it brings peace, and if you can, talk it over with someone wise.

guides.title: Handing over a worry
guides.sub: Doing your part, and leaving the rest with God
guides.about: “Be nothing solicitous,” writes Saint Paul, “but in every thing, by prayer and supplication, with thanksgiving, let your petitions be made known to God.” Saint Francis de Sales calls anxiety the greatest evil that can befall the soul, sin only excepted, because a troubled heart can neither see clearly nor resist well. This prayer takes a few minutes: name the worry, do what is yours, and give the rest to God.

steps.title: Name it
steps.text: Tell God exactly what you are worried about, as it is. Fears grow larger when they stay vague. If it helps, write it down.

steps.title: Hear him
steps.text: Read the Lord’s words slowly. He does not promise that tomorrow will be easy; he tells you that you have a Father who knows what you need.

steps.title: What is yours today
steps.text: Ask whether there is anything you can actually do about this today. If there is, choose one step and decide when you will take it. If there is nothing, that part is not yours to carry today.

steps.title: Give the rest
steps.text: Hand the rest over in plain words: “This I cannot change or control; I give it to you.” Saint Peter says: “Casting all your care upon him, for he hath care of you.” When the worry comes back, as it may, give it again.

steps.title: Trust
steps.text: Make an act of hope slowly, and then go back to the next thing you have to do. “Jesus, I trust in you” is enough when the worry returns.

steps.title: If it does not lift
steps.text: Grace works through nature. If worry is constant, keeps you from sleeping or eating, or comes as panic, see a doctor as you would for any other illness, and talk to someone you trust. That is not a lack of faith.

links.label: When you are anxious or afraid

guides.title: In a moment of temptation
guides.sub: Four short steps, for when it is hard
guides.about: Temptation is not sin: feeling it is not the same as giving in. Saint Francis de Sales gives simple advice for the moment itself: turn to Christ at once, as a child runs to its mother; do not argue with the temptation; and leave it behind by turning to something else. Each step takes less than a minute.

steps.title: Turn to Christ now
steps.text: Turn to him at once, as a child runs to its mother at the first sight of danger. Do not wait until the temptation is stronger. “Watch ye: and pray that ye enter not into temptation.”

steps.title: Call on his name
steps.text: Say the name of Jesus slowly, or this prayer. You need no other words.

steps.title: Do not argue
steps.text: Do not argue with the thought, examine it or look at it closely; that only gives it room. Give it no answer but a turning of your heart to God.

steps.title: Change what you are doing
steps.text: Get up, move, go where there are other people, put the screen down, or do some piece of work. If you resisted, thank God. If you fell, do not despair: make an act of contrition, and begin again.

phraseHint: Stay with these words for as long as they give you something: what they mean, a likeness that comes to mind, a feeling, a reason for thanks. When they have nothing more to give, go on to the next. There is no hurry, and no need to finish.

help.title: When prayer is dry
help.sub: No feeling, no words, no sense of God
counsel: Dryness in prayer is one of the commonest experiences of those who pray seriously, and the saints write about it at length. Saint Teresa of Avila says that for years she spent much of her prayer longing for the hour to end, and still she insists that whoever has begun to pray should never give it up.

Look calmly for a cause, as Saint Francis de Sales advises, without hunting for one: a sin not yet confessed, too little sleep, illness, a life too crowded. Put right what you find. If you find nothing, this may simply be a time of trial, and prayer kept without feeling is, he says, all the more precious. Saint John of the Cross warns that dryness can also come from low spirits or bodily illness: if a heaviness lies over the whole of life, not only prayer, see a doctor too.
Saint Ignatius gives a rule worth remembering: in a time of desolation, make no change to the good resolutions you made before it.

Do not try to decide for yourself what stage of the spiritual life this is. Keep your time of prayer, even if it is short; tell God plainly that it is hard; and speak of it to your confessor if it lasts. Saint Thérèse often fell asleep at prayer and was not troubled by it: a child, she said, is as dear to its parents asleep as awake.
do: Keep your usual time of prayer, even if you shorten it.
Pray slowly with a psalm instead of your own words.
Change nothing you resolved before the dryness began.
If it lasts, speak of it in confession.
from: Saint Teresa of Avila, The Book of Her Life, chapter 8
Saint Francis de Sales, Introduction to the Devout Life, part IV, chapters 14 and 15
Saint John of the Cross, The Dark Night, book I, chapter 9
Saint Ignatius of Loyola, Spiritual Exercises, rules for the discernment of spirits, rule 5
Saint Thérèse of Lisieux, Story of a Soul, Manuscript A

help.title: If you have missed your prayer
help.sub: A day, a week, or longer
counsel: Some days the time for prayer is lost: a sick child, an early start, plain forgetfulness. Saint Francis de Sales’s advice is simple. Make it up later in the day if you can. If you cannot, turn to God in a few short prayers from the heart and read a page of something good, with a word of sorrow for the neglect and a resolve for tomorrow; then let it go.

Then begin again tomorrow. Biblica keeps no streaks and never marks a day as missed, and God does not keep the kind of count we fear. What he asks is that we come back. His mercies, says the prophet, are new every morning.
do: Turn to God now, in a sentence.
Do the next small thing on your list, not all of them at once.
Begin again tomorrow, without trying to make up the whole of today.
from: Saint Francis de Sales, Introduction to the Devout Life, part II, chapter 1

help.title: After a fall
help.sub: When you have sinned, perhaps again
counsel: Everyone who tries to live for God falls, and often in the same place. What matters is what happens next. Saint Francis de Sales asks for a quiet, steady sorrow, not anger with yourself: correct your heart as a father would correct a son, firmly and gently, and begin again. Lorenzo Scupoli, in The Spiritual Combat, reads discouragement after a fall as a sign that we had been trusting in ourselves rather than in God.

Tell God what happened, simply, and ask his pardon. If it was a grave sin, go to confession before you receive Communion. Until you can, make an act of contrition out of love for God, with the resolve to confess as soon as you can; the Church teaches that such contrition already obtains forgiveness (Catechism, 1452).
Remember the father in the parable, who saw his son while he was yet a great way off, and ran to him.
do: Make an act of contrition now.
If it was serious, decide when you will go to confession.
Notice what led to it, without dwelling on it, and change one thing.
Then go back to your day.
from: Saint Francis de Sales, Introduction to the Devout Life, part III, chapter 9
Lorenzo Scupoli, The Spiritual Combat, chapter 4
Catechism of the Catholic Church, 1452

help.title: When you are tempted
help.sub: Feeling it is not the same as giving in
counsel: Temptation is not sin. Saint Francis de Sales distinguishes carefully between the temptation, the pleasure we may feel in it, and consent. However strongly it is felt, and even if some pleasure is felt against our will, there is no sin while the will refuses it; sin begins when we consent, or choose to dwell on the pleasure. A temptation resisted is a victory.

His counsel for strong temptations is to turn at once to Christ, as a child runs to its mother, and not to argue with the temptation or look at it closely. Smaller ones are best given no attention at all: do something else.
Stay away from what you know leads you into it, and tell your confessor about the temptations that keep returning. One that is named before a priest loses much of its hold.
do: Turn to God in a short prayer now.
Get up and change what you are doing.
Stay away from what leads you into it.
Tell your confessor about the ones that keep coming back.
from: Saint Francis de Sales, Introduction to the Devout Life, part IV, chapters 3 to 9

help.title: When you are anxious or afraid
help.sub: Worry about tomorrow, fear of what may come
counsel: Saint Francis de Sales calls anxiety the greatest evil that can befall the soul, sin only excepted, because a troubled heart cannot defend itself. Do calmly what is in your power, he says, and leave the outcome with God.

Name the fear to God as it is. Then do the next thing that is yours to do today, and only that. “Be not therefore solicitous for to morrow,” says the Lord; “sufficient for the day is the evil thereof.”
Grace works through nature. If worry or fear is constant, keeps you from sleeping or eating, or comes as panic, see a doctor as you would for any other illness. That is not a lack of faith.
do: Tell God plainly what you are afraid of.
Do the next small duty in front of you.
Say a short prayer of trust, slowly, several times.
If it does not lift, talk to someone you trust, or to a doctor.
from: Saint Francis de Sales, Introduction to the Devout Life, part IV, chapter 11

help.title: In illness or suffering
help.sub: In pain, or watching someone you love suffer
counsel: Suffering is not a sign that God has forgotten you. Saint Paul rejoiced in his sufferings, because in his own flesh he filled up “those things that are wanting of the sufferings of Christ” for the Church. Joined to Christ’s, your suffering is not wasted. Offer it, for someone or something in particular; Saint John Paul II wrote a whole letter on this, Salvifici Doloris.
Offering it does not mean refusing relief. Use the treatment and the pain relief you need; the Church encourages it.

Ask for the sacraments. Anyone who begins to be in danger through illness or old age may receive the Anointing of the Sick; it is not only for the dying. Illness excuses from Sunday Mass, and Holy Communion can be brought to those who cannot get there. Ask your parish.

When you cannot pray as you used to, short prayers are enough, and so is offering the hours as they come. Let others pray for you. If you are caring for someone who suffers, your care is itself a prayer; let others take a turn so that you can rest.
do: Offer what you are going through for a particular intention.
Ask your parish for Communion at home, or for the Anointing of the Sick.
Pray short prayers, and let others pray for you.
from: Saint John Paul II, Salvifici Doloris (1984)
Catechism of the Catholic Church, on the Anointing of the Sick, Sunday Mass and pain relief
Code of Canon Law, canon 1004

help.title: In grief
help.sub: When someone you love has died
counsel: Jesus wept at the grave of his friend Lazarus, though he was about to raise him. Grief is not a failure of faith. Saint Paul does not tell us not to grieve, but not to be sorrowful “even as others who have no hope.”
Saint Augustine, when his mother Saint Monica died, at first held back his tears; later he let them come, and found rest in them. He asked his readers to remember her at the altar.

Pray for those who have died, and have Mass offered for them: praying for the dead is a work of mercy, and Scripture calls it “a holy and wholesome thought.” Let others help you, and give yourself time.
If you have lost someone to suicide, or a child who died before baptism, the Church entrusts them to the mercy of God, and so may you.
do: Pray for the one you have lost.
Ask your parish to have a Mass offered for them.
Let others help you; you need not be strong alone.
If grief does not ease with time, or takes away sleep and appetite, talk with a priest, a counsellor or a doctor.

from: Saint Augustine, Confessions, book IX, chapters 12 and 13
Catechism of the Catholic Church, on prayer for the dead, suicide and children who die without baptism

help.title: When God seems far, or faith is hard
counsel: Difficulty is not the same as doubt. Saint John Henry Newman wrote that ten thousand difficulties do not make one doubt. Questions can be brought to God; they need not be hidden from him.

Saint Thomas the Apostle doubted, and was answered. Saint Teresa of Calcutta spent most of her years of work without feeling God’s presence, and went on praying and serving. Feelings are not faith: faith holds on to God when they fail.
Keep praying, even if it is only “I do believe, Lord. Help my unbelief.” Read one of the Gospels slowly. Talk to a priest: you are not the first to ask.
do: Pray in a sentence, as you are.
Read a Gospel slowly, a chapter at a time.
Keep going to Mass.
Take your questions to a priest.
from: Saint John Henry Newman, Apologia pro Vita Sua, chapter 5
Biography of Saint Teresa of Calcutta, Holy See, 2003

help.title: When your conscience will not rest
help.sub: Scruples: seeing sin everywhere, never sure of forgiveness
counsel: Some people are troubled by scruples: an anxious conscience that sees sin where there is none, or cannot believe a sin forgiven. It is a known affliction, not a sign of special holiness. Saint Ignatius, who suffered from it, wrote notes on scruples in the Spiritual Exercises; Saint Alphonsus Liguori suffered from it for much of his life.

The remedy the saints give is obedience to one confessor. Follow his guidance even when it does not feel right, and do not confess again sins that have been forgiven. Confessors commonly tell the scrupulous to treat a doubtful sin as not committed and to act against the scruple; follow what yours tells you.
Use this app’s examination of conscience gently: a few questions are enough, and none of it is meant to be read over and over.

When scruples are severe or long-lasting, or spread into the rest of life (checking, repeating, fear of contamination), they can be a form of obsessive-compulsive disorder, an illness that can be treated. See a doctor or therapist as well as your confessor; a good confessor will encourage it. That is not a lack of faith.
do: Choose one confessor, and follow his advice.
Do not confess again what has been forgiven.
Keep the examination short, and leave the rest.
Ask for peace, and go on with your day.
If it does not ease, or spreads beyond confession, talk to a doctor too.
from: Saint Ignatius of Loyola, Spiritual Exercises, notes concerning scruples

help.title: When there is too much to do
help.sub: A crowded day, a hard season
counsel: Saint Francis de Sales asks us to attend to our affairs with care but without eagerness or anxiety: holding on to the work with one hand and to God with the other, as a child walking with its father.

On a crowded day, keep your practices small rather than dropping them: a minute’s offering in the morning, a short prayer at the door and at the desk, a few minutes looking back at night. Brother Lawrence found God among the pots and pans of his kitchen as surely as in church.
Martha was not rebuked for working, but for being “troubled about many things.” One thing is necessary.
do: Offer the day in a sentence before it starts.
Do one thing at a time, and give it your attention.
Pray at the joins of the day: the door, the desk, the kettle.
Look back for a few minutes at night.
from: Saint Francis de Sales, Introduction to the Devout Life, part III, chapter 10
Brother Lawrence, The Practice of the Presence of God, fourth conversation

help.title: When it is all too much
help.sub: Despair, or thoughts of harming yourself
help.urgent: If you are thinking of ending your life or harming yourself, call or text 988 in the United States or Canada, call Samaritans on 116 123 in the United Kingdom or Ireland, or your local emergency number, now. You are not alone, and asking for help is not a failure of faith.
counsel: In your darkest moment you are still loved by God, who “healeth the broken of heart, and bindeth up their bruises.” Many saints knew darkness and the temptation to despair. The prophet Elijah lay down under a tree and asked to die, and God sent an angel with bread and water; he ate and slept, and was fed again. Saint Thérèse, in her last illness, was tormented by temptations against faith.
Despair, and thoughts like these, are often a sign of depression or another illness that can be treated. A doctor can help.
Tell someone today: a friend, your family, a priest, a doctor. You do not have to carry this alone, and you are not meant to.
do: If you are in danger, call or text 988 (United States, Canada), call 116 123 (United Kingdom, Ireland), or your local emergency number.
Tell someone you trust, today.
Pray even a few words: “Jesus, I trust in you.”
from: Saint Thérèse of Lisieux, Story of a Soul, Manuscript C

help.title: In joy and consolation
help.sub: When prayer is sweet and God feels near
counsel: Give thanks. Consolation is God’s gift, Saint Ignatius says, not something we earn or can keep. Receive it simply, thank him for it, and let it make you generous.
He adds two counsels. In consolation, remember that desolation will come, and gather strength for it. And stay humble, remembering how little you could do without grace.
Share your joy. Mary, full of joy, went with haste to her cousin Elizabeth, and sang the Magnificat.
do: Thank God in your own words.
Write down what you are grateful for.
Share the joy with someone.
Do one generous thing while it is easy.
from: Saint Ignatius of Loyola, Spiritual Exercises, rules for the discernment of spirits, rules 9 to 11

help.title: When life is going well
counsel: Plenty has its own danger, which is forgetting the giver. Moses warned the people that when they had eaten and were full, they should bless the Lord, and beware lest they forget him.
Saint Francis de Sales advises being poor in spirit while rich in fact: keep your heart free of what you own, and give generously, to the poor and with your own hands as well as your purse.
Keep your rule of prayer when things are easy. It is then that the habits are formed that will hold when they are not.
do: Thank God for particular gifts, by name.
Give something away this week, generously.
Keep your times of prayer, though you feel less need of them.
Remember someone who is struggling.
from: Saint Francis de Sales, Introduction to the Devout Life, part III, chapters 14 and 15

help.title: At a new beginning
help.sub: Coming back, a new year, Lent, a new chapter of life
counsel: Every day is a beginning, and some days are more so: a return to the sacraments, a new year, the start of Lent, a move, a marriage, a birth. Begin small. Saint Francis de Sales built the Introduction to the Devout Life on a few practices chosen once and then kept: an offering in the morning, a time of prayer, Mass, an examen at night, short prayers through the day.
If you have been away a long time, begin with confession; the priest will help you. Choose a saint to walk with. Then let the rest grow.
“Forgetting the things that are behind,” writes Saint Paul, “and stretching forth myself to those that are before.”
do: Choose two or three things to do each day, and no more for now.
Go to confession if it has been a long time.
Choose a saint to walk with.
After a month, look back and adjust.
from: Saint Francis de Sales, Introduction to the Devout Life, part II

rules.title: As Saint Francis de Sales taught Philothea
rules.sub: For anyone living in the world: a home, a trade, a household
rules.about: In 1609 the Bishop of Geneva wrote the Introduction to the Devout Life for people living in towns, families and courts, and its second part is a whole plan of life: the day offered in the morning, a time of prayer, Mass, short prayers through the day, an evening look back, and the sacraments. He insists that devotion takes a different form in each life and must fit each person’s strength, calling and duties: a parent’s is not a monk’s. Begin with a few of these and add the rest slowly.

quote.text: A different exercise of devotion is required of each—the noble, the artisan, the servant, the prince, the maiden and the wife; and furthermore such practice must be modified according to the strength, the calling, and the duties of each individual.
quote.source: Introduction to the Devout Life, I.3 (anonymous nineteenth-century translation, Library of Spiritual Works for English Catholics)

rules.caution: His counsels on fasting and bodily penance are left out, since he wanted none taken on without the advice of a confessor or director.

entries.why: He advises an hour, early if you can; a quarter of an hour is a real beginning.

entries.why: He urges daily Mass where possible, and when you cannot go, joining it in spirit at some hour of the morning.
entries.source: Introduction to the Devout Life, II.14

entries.title: Sunday Mass
entries.why: He counsels receiving Communion every Sunday.
entries.source: Introduction to the Devout Life, II.20

entries.title: Retiring into the heart
entries.why: Now and then through the day, withdraw into your heart to God, even at work or in company.
entries.source: Introduction to the Devout Life, II.12

entries.title: Short prayers through the day
entries.why: Brief lifts of the heart to God, in your own words rather than set forms.
entries.source: Introduction to the Devout Life, II.13

entries.title: Spiritual reading
entries.why: A little of a good book each day, read as if it were a letter from the saints.
entries.source: Introduction to the Devout Life, II.17

entries.title: Work done calmly, one hand in God’s
entries.why: Careful in your affairs but not anxious, like a child holding its father’s hand while it picks berries with the other.
entries.source: Introduction to the Devout Life, III.10

entries.title: Evening examen
entries.why: Thank God for the day, look over it, ask pardon, and commend yourself and your household to him.
entries.source: Introduction to the Devout Life, II.11

entries.title: Gentle with myself after a fault
entries.why: A quiet, steady displeasure at your faults, never irritation with yourself.
entries.source: Introduction to the Devout Life, III.9

entries.why: He advised it every week; how often is right for you is a question for your confessor.
entries.source: Introduction to the Devout Life, II.19

entries.why: Once a year the heart taken apart and cleaned like a clock; his feast day is suggested, but any fitting day will do.
entries.source: Introduction to the Devout Life, V.1

rules.title: Saint John Henry Newman’s short road
rules.sub: For anyone who wants the ordinary day done well
rules.about: In a short note of 1856 Newman wrote that perfection is not some extraordinary service but the ordinary duties of the day done well, and then said what that means from rising to bed. His list is meant to simplify a life, not to load it: ordinary things, done well, for God. Keep what your own day allows.

quote.text: He, then, is perfect who does the work of the day perfectly, and we need not go beyond this to seek for perfection.
quote.source: Newman, “A Short Road to Perfection” (27 September 1856), in Meditations and Devotions

rules.caution: Keeping out bad thoughts means turning away from them, not fretting over every one that passes; a temptation is not a sin.
sources: John Henry Newman, “A Short Road to Perfection”, dated 27 September 1856, in Meditations and Devotions (Longmans, Green, 1907 impression), pp. 285–286: https://www.newmanreader.org/works/meditations/meditations8.html#shortroad

entries.title: The day’s ordinary duties done well
entries.why: His whole point: perfection is the work of the day done well, not something beyond it.
entries.source: A Short Road to Perfection (1856)

entries.title: Rise on time
entries.why: Get up at the time you meant to, without lingering in bed.
entries.source: A Short Road to Perfection (1856)

entries.title: First thoughts to God
entries.why: Before the day takes hold, turn your first thoughts to God.
entries.source: A Short Road to Perfection (1856)

entries.title: A good visit to the Blessed Sacrament
entries.why: A visit to a church, made well rather than hurried.
entries.source: A Short Road to Perfection (1856)

entries.title: The Angelus, said devoutly
entries.why: The Angelus said with attention, not hurried.
entries.source: A Short Road to Perfection (1856)

entries.title: Eat and drink to God’s glory
entries.why: Meals taken with thanks and for God’s glory.
entries.source: A Short Road to Perfection (1856); 1 Corinthians 10:31

entries.title: The Rosary, said well
entries.why: Said well rather than quickly; one decade said well is a start.
entries.source: A Short Road to Perfection (1856)

entries.title: Be recollected
entries.why: Keep your heart gathered and turned to God amid the day’s business.
entries.source: A Short Road to Perfection (1856)

entries.title: Keep out bad thoughts
entries.why: Turn from a bad thought quietly as soon as you notice it, and go on.
entries.source: A Short Road to Perfection (1856)

entries.title: Evening meditation
entries.why: A time of silent prayer in the evening, made well.
entries.source: A Short Road to Perfection (1856)

entries.title: Examine yourself daily
entries.why: A daily look back over the day before God.
entries.source: A Short Road to Perfection (1856)

entries.title: Bed in good time
entries.why: Go to bed in good time, so that tomorrow can begin well.
entries.source: A Short Road to Perfection (1856)

rules.title: As Saint Alphonsus taught
rules.sub: For anyone who wants a full rule, taken on little by little
rules.about: Alphonsus Liguori (1696–1787), a Neapolitan lawyer who became a priest, founded the Redemptorists and later served as a bishop, wrote for ordinary believers and taught that whoever prays is saved. His short Rule of Life asks for a few acts on waking, meditation, Mass, reading, a daily visit to the Blessed Sacrament and to Our Lady, an evening examen, and the sacraments. He makes room for circumstances himself (“if your state of life allow it”), so take a few of these first and let the rest come later.

quote.text: Say her Litanies, and the Rosary, meditating on the mysteries.
quote.source: Saint Alphonsus, Rule of Life (abridged), in The Way of Salvation and of Perfection, ed. Eugene Grimm

rules.caution: His fasts on Saturdays and on the eves of Our Lady’s feasts are left out: he asks that they be undertaken only on a confessor’s advice.
sources: Saint Alphonsus de Liguori, The Way of Salvation and of Perfection, ed. Eugene Grimm, Complete Ascetical Works vol. entries.why: Adore God, offer him the day, resolve to avoid sin; then three Hail Marys in honour of Our Lady’s purity.
entries.source: Rule of Life (abridged), in The Way of Salvation and of Perfection

entries.title: Meditation

entries.title: Mass on weekdays, when I can

entries.why: Some reading from a spiritual book each day, the lives of the saints especially.

rules.title: Saint Josemaría’s plan of life
rules.sub: For people seeking holiness in ordinary work and family life
rules.about: Josemaría Escrivá (1902–1975), a Spanish priest who founded Opus Dei, taught that ordinary work and family life are themselves a way to holiness. The plan of life that Opus Dei describes is a handful of practices of piety set into a working day, and it presents them as something to adapt to each person’s circumstances. This is a short summary in our own words: choose a few and let the rest wait.
rules.caution: The plan is meant to be fitted to each person’s day; take only what fits yours.

rules.title: Saint Thérèse’s little way
rules.sub: Interior habits for any life, carried through the day
rules.about: Thérèse Martin (1873–1897), a Carmelite nun of Lisieux who died at twenty-four, found a little way for people who feel too small for great things: small acts done for love, sacrifices no one sees, and complete trust in God’s mercy. These are not prayers to add but ways of meeting the day, and they fit any state of life. She herself was not allowed the bodily penances she felt drawn to, and wrote that mortifying her self-love did her far more good.

quote.text: One of God’s gifts was a great attraction towards penance, but I was not permitted to satisfy it; the only mortification allowed me consisted in mortifying my self-love, and this did me far more good than bodily penance would have done.
quote.source: Saint Thérèse, Story of a Soul, ch. VII (T. N. Taylor’s edition, London, 1912)

rules.caution: These are dispositions, not tasks to tick; not excusing yourself means letting small, unjust blame pass, never hiding the truth when it matters or putting up with harm.
sources: Soeur Thérèse of Lisieux, the Little Flower of Jesus, ed. T. N. Taylor (Burns, Oates & Washbourne, London; imprimatur 9 December 1912), ch. VII, VIII, IX, XI and Counsels and Reminiscences: https://ccel.org/ccel/therese/autobio.iii.html

entries.title: The Gospel of the day

entries.source: Story of a Soul, ch. VIII

entries.title: Small sacrifices no one sees
entries.why: Little hidden acts, such as folding what others forgot or quietly helping, with no one the wiser.
entries.source: Story of a Soul, ch. VII and XI

entries.title: Small things done for love
entries.why: The smallest actions of the day done for love of God, letting no look or word go by.
entries.source: Story of a Soul, ch. XI

entries.title: Kindness to the one I find hardest
entries.why: Pray for that person, do them the services you would do a friend, and smile rather than answer sharply.
entries.source: Story of a Soul, ch. IX

entries.title: Not excusing myself
entries.why: When blamed unfairly in a small matter, let it pass and keep your peace.
entries.source: Story of a Soul, ch. IX; Counsels and Reminiscences

entries.title: After a fault, trust and begin again
entries.why: Bear with your own imperfections and let Jesus carry you where you cannot climb.

rules.title: In the house of Saint Thomas More
rules.sub: For a husband, father and professional with a public life
rules.about: Thomas More (1478–1535), a London lawyer, husband and father who became Lord Chancellor of England, died a martyr for refusing to accept the king as head of the Church in England. His son-in-law William Roper describes a household that prayed together every day, Fridays given to prayer, and confession and Communion before any weighty business. Saint Francis de Sales’s rule applies to his example: take what fits a family and a working life, not what he did under his own conscience in another age.
rules.caution: Leave out his hair shirt and his very early rising: Saint Francis de Sales judged the hair shirt “not fit for ordinary people, married persons”, and wanted everyone to sleep as much as health and work require.

rules.about: Louis Martin (1823–1894), a watchmaker, and Zélie Guérin (1831–1877), who made Alençon lace, were the parents of Saint Thérèse and were canonised together in 2015. Their daughter remembered Sunday Mass with the whole family, walks with a visit to the Blessed Sacrament, alms given to beggars and night prayers together; the 1912 account of the family adds daily Mass, the Church’s fasts kept faithfully and Sunday as a day of rest. Their devotion fitted a shop and a houseful of children; take what fits your home.

rules.title: With Saint Pier Giorgio Frassati
rules.sub: For students and young adults, with friends and the outdoors
rules.about: Pier Giorgio Frassati (1901–1925), a mining-engineering student in Turin, spent his free time with the poor through the Saint Vincent de Paul Society, loved climbing mountains with his friends, and died of polio at twenty-four; he was canonised on 7 September 2025. His faith was joyful and practical: the Eucharist, the Rosary, and the poor visited in person. He lived it as a layman with exams, friends and a father who did not share his faith, so it fits a full young life.
rules.caution: His nights of adoration and his habit of giving away what he had were his own generosity, not rules for anyone else.

rules.title: With Saint Carlo Acutis
rules.sub: For teenagers, and anyone growing up online
rules.about: Carlo Acutis (1991–2006), a schoolboy in Milan who taught himself programming and built a website on the Eucharistic miracles, died at fifteen and was canonised on 7 September 2025. He put the Eucharist at the centre of an ordinary teenager’s life and set himself a limit on video games. Much of what is told of his daily habits comes from his mother’s testimony; take them as a young man’s own free choices, fitted to his life, not as a rule for every teenager.
rules.caution: Daily Mass and weekly confession were his own choices; for most young people Sunday Mass and regular confession are the place to start.

rules.title: With Saint Ignatius: the examen
rules.sub: A few minutes morning, midday and night, for anyone
rules.about: Ignatius of Loyola (1491–1556), a Basque soldier who became a priest and founded the Society of Jesus, wrote the Spiritual Exercises and insisted that what is given be fitted to each person. From them come the daily examination of conscience, which begins with thanks, and a short way of working on one fault at a time. His rules for discernment add an interior habit for hard days: in desolation, change none of your good resolutions.

quote.text: The first Point is to give thanks to God our Lord for the benefits received.
quote.source: Saint Ignatius, Spiritual Exercises, General Examen of Conscience (tr. Elder Mullan, New York, 1914)

rules.caution: The particular examen is for one fault at a time and for a limited time, best with your confessor’s advice; leave it out if you are prone to scruples.
