chaplets.name: The Chaplet of Divine Mercy
chaplets.sub: On the beads of the Rosary; traditionally at three in the afternoon
about: In 1935 Saint Faustina Kowalska, a Polish nun, was taught this prayer, which she recorded in her Diary. It offers to the Father the sacrifice of his Son on behalf of the whole world, and asks mercy for it. Saint John Paul II canonised her in 2000 and set the Second Sunday of Easter as Divine Mercy Sunday.

It takes about ten minutes. Many pray it at three in the afternoon, the hour of Christ’s death, and on the nine days before Divine Mercy Sunday as a novena. Say it slowly: the same words return fifty times so that the heart can rest in them.
chaplets.note: The English of the chaplet is the app’s own translation of Saint Faustina’s Polish.

habits.title: The presence of God
habits.sub: Turning to him often, wherever you are
what: God is everywhere, holding all things in being, and, as Saint Francis de Sales says, he is present in a very special way in your own heart. This habit is simply remembering it: turning to him for a moment, many times a day, at the door, at the desk, at the sink, between one thing and the next.

Brother Lawrence, a lay brother who worked for years in a monastery kitchen, made this his whole method, and found that work and prayer stopped being two separate things. Saint Francis de Sales recommends the same to people in the world: short movements of the heart towards God, in your own words, woven into the day without hindering it.

saints.text: The time of business does not with me differ from the time of prayer.
saints.by: Brother Lawrence, The Practice of the Presence of God, fourth conversation

saints.text: Do you then, my daughter, aspire continually to God, by brief, ardent upliftings of heart.
saints.by: Saint Francis de Sales, Introduction to the Devout Life, part II, chapter 13

how: Choose two or three moments that come every day, such as going through a door, sitting down to work or waiting for the kettle, and let each be a reminder to turn to God.
At each one, say a word to him in your own way: thanks, a request, an act of love, or simply his name.
Before a task, ask his help; when it is done, thank him.
When you notice you have forgotten him for hours, do not scold yourself. Turn back to him and carry on.
habits.start: Choose one doorway you pass through every day, and say a word to God each time you go through it.
habits.examine: When did I remember God today, even for a moment, and what was happening when I forgot him?
habits.caution: This is not a matter of strain or of thinking about God every second; turning back gently whenever you notice is the whole of the practice.
from: Brother Lawrence, The Practice of the Presence of God (Revell, 1895), second and fourth conversations
Saint Francis de Sales, Introduction to the Devout Life, part II, chapters 2, 12 and 13

habits.title: The duty of the moment
habits.sub: The next thing, done well, for God
what: Holiness is not found somewhere else, in a life you do not have. It is found in what this moment asks: the work in front of you, the person who needs you, the trouble you did not choose. Jean-Pierre de Caussade called this the sacrament of the present moment: God gives himself to us under the plain appearance of ordinary duties.

The habit is to stop living half in yesterday and half in tomorrow, and to give yourself, for God, to what you are doing now. Saint John Henry Newman put it simply: perfection is doing the work of the day well.

saints.text: That which comes to us each moment by the order of God is best and holiest and most divine for us.
saints.by: Jean-Pierre de Caussade, Abandonment to Divine Providence, book I, chapter 4 (tr. Ella McMahon, 1887)

saints.text: He, then, is perfect who does the work of the day perfectly, and we need not go beyond this to seek for perfection.
saints.by: Saint John Henry Newman, “A Short Road to Perfection” (1856)

saints.text: Do what you have to do, and put yourself wholly into it.
saints.by: Saint Josemaría Escrivá, The Way, 815 (our paraphrase)

how: When you begin something, ask what this moment asks of you, and do that, not three things at once.
Offer the task to God in a word before you start.
When your mind runs ahead to tomorrow or back to yesterday, bring it back to the thing in your hands.
As far as you can, treat interruptions as part of the duty rather than its enemy.
habits.start: Before the next ordinary task, say “This, for you”, and then give it your full attention.
habits.examine: Was there a moment today when I was wholly present to what I was doing, or to the person in front of me?
habits.caution: The duty of the moment includes rest, meals and sleep; it is not a call to fill every minute.
from: Jean-Pierre de Caussade, Abandonment to Divine Providence, book I, chapters 2, 4, 5 and 8 (tr. Ella McMahon, Benziger, 1887)
Saint John Henry Newman, Meditations and Devotions, “A Short Road to Perfection”
Saint Josemaría Escrivá, The Way, 815 (summarised)

habits.title: The heroic minute
habits.sub: Rising when it is time, and giving God the first thought
what: Saint Josemaría Escrivá called the moment of getting up “the heroic minute”: the time comes, and you rise at once, without bargaining, with a thought for God. It is a very small victory, but it is won at the start of the day, and it trains the will for everything that follows.
Newman put rising on time first in his short road to perfection, and joined it to giving your first thoughts to God. The first minutes of the day often set its tone.

saints.text: Do not lie in bed beyond the due time of rising; give your first thoughts to God.
saints.by: Saint John Henry Newman, “A Short Road to Perfection” (1856)

saints.text: I think it is wise to go to sleep early at night in order to be ready to waken and rise early.
saints.by: Saint Francis de Sales, Introduction to the Devout Life, part III, chapter 23

how: Decide the night before what time you will get up, and go to bed early enough to make it possible.
When the time comes, get up at once, before you start to argue with yourself.
Let your first words be to God: the Sign of the Cross, “Thanks be to God”, or the morning offering.
Leave the phone out of reach until you have greeted God.
habits.start: Tomorrow, when you wake at the time you chose, sit up at once and make the Sign of the Cross.
habits.examine: How did I begin this day, and what would help me begin tomorrow better?
habits.caution: If you are ill, exhausted, caring for someone through the night or low in spirits, enough sleep is the duty; this is a counsel, never a rule.
from: Saint John Henry Newman, Meditations and Devotions, “A Short Road to Perfection” (1856)
Saint Josemaría Escrivá, on “the heroic minute” (summarised)
Saint Francis de Sales, Introduction to the Devout Life, part III, chapter 23

habits.title: No complaining
habits.sub: Letting small troubles pass without a word
what: Much complaining is about small things: the weather, the queue, the traffic, the food, other people’s habits. It rarely changes anything, it spreads gloom, and it keeps the mind turned on itself. Saint Francis de Sales often said that whoever complains seldom does so without sinning, because self-love always makes our own troubles look larger than they are.

The habit is to let the small annoyances of the day go by in silence, or to give them to God, and to keep real complaints for those who can do something about them. It makes room for patience, gratitude and good humour.

saints.text: A really patient man neither complains nor seeks to be pitied.
saints.by: Saint Francis de Sales, Introduction to the Devout Life, part III, chapter 3

saints.text: He who complains, seldom does so without sinning.
saints.by: Saint Francis de Sales, one of his frequent sayings, in Jean-Pierre Camus, The Spirit of St. Francis de Sales (tr. 1910)

how: Notice the small complaints that come out of habit: about weather, delays, food, other people.
When one rises, let it pass unspoken, or turn it into a word to God: “This too, for you.”
If something really needs to change, say so calmly, once, to the person who can change it.
When you are tempted to complain about someone, say something good about them instead, or nothing.
habits.start: Let one small annoyance today go by without a word, and offer it to God.
habits.examine: Did I complain today about something small, and what was underneath it?
habits.caution: Not complaining never means hiding pain from a doctor, keeping silent about abuse or injustice, or refusing to ask for help; Saint Francis de Sales allowed all of these, done calmly.
from: Saint Francis de Sales, Introduction to the Devout Life, part III, chapter 3
Jean-Pierre Camus, The Spirit of St. Francis de Sales (tr. J. S., 1910), “That he who complains sins”

habits.title: Guarding the tongue
habits.sub: No gossip, no running down of others
what: Saint James says that whoever does not offend in word is a perfect man. Much harm is done by talk: making known another’s faults without need, saying what is untrue about them, or the easy pleasure of gossip that leaves someone smaller than before. The Church teaches that a person’s good name is owed to them in justice.

The habit is a guard on the mouth: to speak of others as you would if they were in the room, to say nothing of their faults without a real reason, and to turn a conversation elsewhere when it turns against someone who is absent.

saints.text: My daughter, I entreat you never speak evil of any, either directly or indirectly.
saints.by: Saint Francis de Sales, Introduction to the Devout Life, part III, chapter 29

saints.text: Nothing must be said to injure another’s character or to find fault.
saints.by: Saint Ignatius of Loyola, Spiritual Exercises, general examen (tr. Elder Mullan, 1914)

how: Before speaking of someone who is not there, ask: is it true, is it kind, and is there a real need to say it?
When a conversation turns to someone’s faults, change the subject, or say something good about them.
When you hear evil of someone, Saint Francis de Sales advises, cast what doubt you fairly can upon it.
If you have harmed someone’s good name, put it right as far as you can.
habits.start: For one day, say nothing about anyone absent that you would not say in front of them.
habits.examine: Did I speak of anyone today in a way I would not want them to hear?
habits.caution: Guarding the tongue does not forbid reporting wrongdoing, protecting someone from harm, or telling those who need to know; that is not detraction.
from: Saint Francis de Sales, Introduction to the Devout Life, part III, chapters 27 to 30
Saint Ignatius of Loyola, Spiritual Exercises, general examen, on words
Catechism of the Catholic Church, 2477 to 2479

habits.title: Thinking well of others
habits.sub: Giving them the benefit of the doubt
what: Most of our judgements of others are made quickly and on little evidence: a tone of voice, a late reply, a look. Saint Ignatius opens the Spiritual Exercises with a rule that is good for every day: be readier to put a good meaning on what another says than to condemn it, and if you cannot, ask what they meant.

This habit works in the mind before it reaches the tongue. It assumes good will until there is real reason not to, and it remembers, with Saint Francis de Sales, that each of us has enough to do in judging ourselves.

saints.text: Let it be presupposed that every good Christian is to be more ready to save his neighbor’s proposition than to condemn it.
saints.by: Saint Ignatius of Loyola, Spiritual Exercises, presupposition (tr. Elder Mullan, 1914)

saints.text: Each one has enough to do in judging himself, without undertaking to judge his neighbour.
saints.by: Saint Francis de Sales, Introduction to the Devout Life, part III, chapter 28

saints.text: Thus it is evident how seldom we weigh our neighbour in the same balance with ourselves.
saints.by: Thomas à Kempis, The Following of Christ, book I, chapter 16 (tr. Challoner)

how: When someone’s words or actions annoy you, look for the most charitable explanation that fits the facts.
If you cannot find one, ask them what they meant before you decide.
Notice when you are reading someone’s mind, and stop.
Think of one good thing about the person you are tempted to judge.
habits.start: The next time someone irritates you, find one generous explanation for what they did before you think anything else.
habits.examine: Whom did I judge quickly today, and is there a kinder way to see what happened?
habits.caution: Thinking well of others does not mean ignoring clear evidence or real danger; prudence still applies.
from: Saint Ignatius of Loyola, Spiritual Exercises, 22
Saint Francis de Sales, Introduction to the Devout Life, part III, chapter 28
Thomas à Kempis, The Following of Christ, book I, chapter 16 (tr. Richard Challoner)
Catechism of the Catholic Church, 2478

habits.title: Kindness to the one you find hardest
habits.sub: Saint Thérèse’s way with a sister who annoyed her
what: In most lives there is someone we find hard: a colleague, a neighbour, a relative whose every habit grates. Saint Thérèse had such a sister in her convent. She did not wait to feel differently. She decided to treat her as she would treat the person she loved most: she prayed for her whenever they met, did her small services, and smiled when she was tempted to answer sharply.

The sister never guessed the struggle, and one day asked Thérèse what attracted her so much. What attracted her, Thérèse wrote, was Jesus hidden in the depths of that soul. Charity, she says, must show itself in deeds and not only in feelings.

saints.text: I set myself to do for this sister all I should do for the one I loved most.
saints.by: Saint Thérèse of Lisieux, Story of a Soul, chapter 9 (tr. T. N. Taylor, 1912)

saints.text: Every time I met her I prayed for her, and offered to God her virtues and merits.
saints.by: Saint Thérèse of Lisieux, Story of a Soul, chapter 9 (tr. T. N. Taylor, 1912)

how: Name to God, privately, the person you find hardest at present.
Pray for them by name each day, and each time you see them, ask God to bless them.
Do them one small kindness they would not expect, without drawing attention to it.
When you are tempted to answer sharply, smile if you can, or change the subject.
habits.start: Tonight, pray for the person you find hardest by name, and ask one good thing for them.
habits.examine: How did I treat the person I find hardest today, in thought, word and deed?
habits.caution: This is for ordinary friction, not for staying close to someone who harms you; from a safe distance, kindness may be prayer alone, and that is enough.
from: Saint Thérèse of Lisieux, Story of a Soul, chapter 9 (tr. T. N. Taylor, Burns, Oates and Washbourne, 1912)

habits.title: Forgiving quickly
habits.sub: Not letting the sun go down on anger
what: Small hurts come every day: a careless word, a slight, someone else’s bad mood. Left alone, they harden into grudges. Saint Paul’s rule is short: “Let not the sun go down upon your anger.” Saint Francis de Sales adds that when anger has got the better of us, we should make up for it quickly by an act of gentleness towards the person concerned.

Forgiveness is an act of the will, not a feeling. The Catechism says that we cannot always help feeling an offence or remembering it; what we can do is refuse to hold it against the other, and turn the hurt into prayer for them. Done quickly and often in small things, it makes the great forgivings possible.

saints.text: Atone for the fault by some speedy act of meekness towards the person who excited your anger.
saints.by: Saint Francis de Sales, Introduction to the Devout Life, part III, chapter 8

how: When someone hurts you, say inwardly as soon as you can: “I forgive them. Lord, bless them.”
Before you sleep, let go of the day’s grudges one by one, with the Our Father.
If you were angry, make peace quickly: a kind word, a small service, an apology for your own part.
If the hurt comes back, forgive again; needing to do it many times is not failure.
habits.start: Tonight, name one person who annoyed or hurt you today, and say: “I forgive them.”
habits.examine: Am I carrying any resentment from today, however small, into the night?
habits.caution: Forgiving does not require warm feelings, trusting again at once, or staying where you are harmed; for deep wounds, the guided prayer “Forgiving someone” goes more slowly.
from: Saint Francis de Sales, Introduction to the Devout Life, part III, chapter 8
Catechism of the Catholic Church, 2840 to 2845

habits.title: Not excusing yourself
habits.sub: Taking correction and small injustices quietly
what: When we are corrected, or blamed for something small, the first reflex is to explain, justify and defend. Saint Thérèse saw that if she began to justify herself she would lose her peace of mind, and she learned to let small misjudgements pass. She found that silence gave more peace than winning the argument.

The habit has two sides: to receive correction without bristling, asking first whether it is true; and to let small, unfair blame go, offering it to God. It is humility in practice: being willing to be thought less of.

saints.text: When misunderstood and judged unfavourably, what benefit do we derive from defending ourselves? Leave things as they are, and say nothing.
saints.by: Saint Thérèse of Lisieux, Counsels and Reminiscences, in Story of a Soul (tr. T. N. Taylor, 1912)

saints.text: We would have others strictly corrected: but are not willing to be corrected ourselves.
saints.by: Thomas à Kempis, The Following of Christ, book I, chapter 16 (tr. Challoner)

how: When you are corrected, say “Thank you” first, and consider afterwards whether it is true.
When blamed for something small, resist the urge to explain unless the explanation is really needed.
If the correction was just, accept it simply; if not, offer the small injustice to God.
Do not keep replaying the conversation to prove yourself right.
habits.start: The next time you are corrected, even about something trivial, say “Thank you” and nothing more for now.
habits.examine: Was I corrected or misjudged today, and how did I answer, outwardly and inwardly?
habits.caution: Letting small misjudgements pass is not the same as keeping silent about serious injustice, abuse, or what others need to know; then speak, calmly and truthfully.
from: Saint Thérèse of Lisieux, Story of a Soul, chapter 9, and Counsels and Reminiscences (tr. T. N. Taylor, 1912)
Thomas à Kempis, The Following of Christ, book I, chapter 16

habits.title: Small hidden sacrifices
habits.sub: Little things given to God that no one sees
what: Saint Thérèse’s little way is made of small things done with great love: picking up a thread, letting someone else have the better place, eating what is put in front of you, holding back a clever remark. They cost little and nobody notices them, and that is part of their worth: they are for God alone.

Saint Francis de Sales says that great occasions to serve God come seldom, but little ones surround us every day. These small renunciations train the will, loosen the hold of comfort and self-love, and keep the heart turned towards God.

saints.text: If you feel too lazy to pick up a bit of thread, and yet do so for love of Jesus, you acquire more merit than for a much nobler action done in a moment of fervour.
saints.by: Saint Thérèse of Lisieux, Counsels and Reminiscences, in Story of a Soul (tr. T. N. Taylor, 1912)

saints.text: We ought not to be weary of doing little things for the love of God, who regards not the greatness of the work, but the love with which it is performed.
saints.by: Brother Lawrence, The Practice of the Presence of God, fourth conversation

saints.text: Great occasions for serving God come seldom, but little ones surround us daily.
saints.by: Saint Francis de Sales, Introduction to the Devout Life, part III, chapter 35

how: Choose one small thing each day to give up or to do for love: no sugar in the coffee, the dull job someone else would have done, the last word left unsaid.
Eat what is put before you without comment; Saint Francis de Sales thought this worth more than fasts of your own choosing.
Tell no one, and keep no count.
Offer each one to God in a word, for someone in need.
habits.start: Today, do one small unseen thing for someone else, and tell no one.
habits.examine: What small thing did I give to God today that no one else saw?
habits.caution: Choose small things that harm neither your health nor your duties, and do not keep adding to them; bodily austerities are not for anyone without a confessor’s advice.
from: Saint Thérèse of Lisieux, Story of a Soul, chapter 9, and Counsels and Reminiscences
Brother Lawrence, The Practice of the Presence of God, fourth conversation
Saint Francis de Sales, Introduction to the Devout Life, part III, chapters 23 and 35

habits.title: Custody of the eyes and of screens
habits.sub: Choosing what you look at
what: What we look at shapes what we think about, and what we think about shapes what we love. The old phrase “custody of the eyes” meant a quiet discipline over what we let in: not staring, not looking at what stirs lust, envy or idle curiosity. Today most of what we look at comes through a screen, much of it designed to hold our attention for as long as possible.

This habit belongs to the virtue of temperance. It does not reject good things; it decides when, how much and what. Carlo Acutis, the teenager who loved computers and used them to spread the faith, is remembered for limiting himself to about an hour of video games a week.

saints.text: Why wilt thou see what thou must not have?
saints.by: Thomas à Kempis, The Following of Christ, book I, chapter 20 (tr. Challoner)

saints.text: Carlo Acutis, who died in 2006 at fifteen, allowed himself about an hour of video games a week, as a discipline.
saints.by: As recounted by his family and those who knew him (our summary)

how: Decide in advance when you will use your phone for things other than work or people, and for how long.
Keep screens out of the bedroom, or at least out of the first and last half hour of the day.
When something you should not look at appears, look away at once, without examining it.
Before opening an app out of habit, pause and ask whether you really want to.
habits.start: Tonight, put your phone in another room half an hour before you go to sleep.
habits.examine: What did I look at today that left me restless, envious or troubled in heart, and what did me good?
habits.caution: If a habit has become compulsive, pornography for instance, bring it to confession and look for practical help as well; willpower alone is rarely the whole remedy, and there is no cause for despair.
from: Thomas à Kempis, The Following of Christ, book I, chapter 20
On Carlo Acutis: accounts from his family and the postulation, as reported by Catholic News Agency (secondary)

habits.title: Gratitude in the moment
habits.sub: Thanking God as things happen
what: Saint Ignatius makes thanks the first point of the examen: to give thanks to God for the benefits received. This habit carries that thanks into the day itself: noticing a gift when it comes, and saying thank you then, not only at night.

Gratitude changes how we see. It is hard to be resentful and thankful at the same time. It also guards against forgetting the Giver when things go well, and keeps us aware that everything, even the next breath, is given.

saints.text: The first Point is to give thanks to God our Lord for the benefits received.
saints.by: Saint Ignatius of Loyola, Spiritual Exercises, general examen (tr. Elder Mullan, 1914)

saints.text: Be grateful then for the least, and thou shalt be worthy to receive greater things.
saints.by: Thomas à Kempis, The Following of Christ, book II, chapter 10 (tr. Challoner)

how: When something good happens, however small, say “Thanks be to God” inwardly, then and there.
Thank people too, by name and for something particular.
At meals, let grace be real thanks, not a formula.
On a hard day, look for one gift in it and thank God for that.
habits.start: Today, thank God silently for three small things at the moment they happen.
habits.examine: What was I given today, and did I notice it at the time?
habits.caution: Gratitude is not pretending that hard things are good; you can thank God for his gifts on a hard day without thanking him for what hurts.
from: Saint Ignatius of Loyola, Spiritual Exercises, general examen, first point
Thomas à Kempis, The Following of Christ, book II, chapter 10

habits.title: Handing over worries
habits.sub: Doing what is yours today, and leaving the rest with God
what: Worry fastens on what we cannot control: tomorrow, other people’s choices, how things will turn out. Saint Paul’s answer is not to stop caring, but to turn each care into prayer, with thanksgiving, and to receive the peace of God in exchange. Christ says that each day has trouble enough of its own.

Saint Francis de Sales calls anxiety the greatest evil that can befall the soul, sin only excepted, because a troubled heart cannot see clearly or resist well. His remedy is to do calmly what is in our power and leave the outcome to God. This habit practises that exchange, many times a day if need be.

saints.text: This unresting anxiety is the greatest evil which can happen to the soul, sin only excepted.
saints.by: Saint Francis de Sales, Introduction to the Devout Life, part IV, chapter 11

saints.text: He does nothing in vain; he may prolong my life, he may shorten it; he knows what he is about.
saints.by: Saint John Henry Newman, Meditations on Christian Doctrine, “Hope in God—Creator”

how: When a worry comes, name it to God in a sentence.
Ask whether there is anything you can do about it today. If there is, decide what and when; if there is not, it is not yours to carry today.
Hand the rest over in words: “This I give to you.” When it comes back, give it again.
Then turn to the next ordinary thing you have to do.
habits.start: The next time you catch yourself worrying, say “Jesus, I trust in you”, and do the next small task in front of you.
habits.examine: What did I worry about today, and did I give it to God?
habits.caution: When anxiety is heavy, constant or comes as panic, see a doctor as well as praying; grace works through medicine too, and needing it is not a lack of faith.
from: Saint Francis de Sales, Introduction to the Devout Life, part IV, chapter 11
Saint John Henry Newman, Meditations and Devotions, “Hope in God—Creator”

habits.title: Patience with yourself
habits.sub: Beginning again after a fault, without anger
what: After a fault there are two ways of being sorry. One is anxious, angry and wounded in pride: how could I have done that again? The other is quiet, steady and humble, and turns at once to God. Saint Francis de Sales wants the second. He tells us to correct our own heart as a good parent corrects a child, firmly but gently, and to begin again.

Brother Lawrence, when he failed, told God that he would always do so if left to himself, asked for help, and gave himself no further uneasiness about it. This habit is that same short road back: sorrow, trust and a fresh start, without a long detour through self-reproach.

saints.text: What we want is a quiet, steady, firm displeasure at our own faults.
saints.by: Saint Francis de Sales, Introduction to the Devout Life, part III, chapter 9

saints.text: Repentance is an effect of love of God, anxiety is an effect of self-love.
saints.by: Carlo Giuseppe Quadrupani, Light and Peace, chapter 5 (tr. 1898)

saints.text: Have patience with everyone, but first of all with yourself.
saints.by: Saint Francis de Sales, as quoted in Quadrupani, Light and Peace (shortened)

how: When you notice a fault, tell God simply: “I am sorry; help me.”
Then go back to what you were doing, without replaying it.
Speak to yourself as you would to a friend who had done the same.
Bring grave sins to confession, and leave the rest to God’s mercy.
habits.start: The next time you catch yourself in a fault, say “Lord, I am sorry; help me”, and carry on without another word of reproach.
habits.examine: When I failed today, how did I treat myself afterwards?
habits.caution: This is not indifference to sin: grave sin still goes to confession, but it goes there with trust, not with self-hatred.
from: Saint Francis de Sales, Introduction to the Devout Life, part III, chapter 9
Brother Lawrence, The Practice of the Presence of God, second conversation
Carlo Giuseppe Quadrupani, Light and Peace, chapter 5 (Herder, 1898)

habits.title: Patience with others
habits.sub: Bearing with their faults, as they bear with ours
what: Everyone we live and work with has faults that try us, as ours try them. Thomas à Kempis says that what we cannot amend in others we must bear with patience, remembering that we too have many things others must put up with. Saint Paul calls it bearing one another’s burdens.

Saint Thérèse came to see that true charity consists in bearing with the defects of others, not being surprised at their weakness, and being edified by their smallest virtues. Patience here is not grim endurance; it is love that refuses to be worn out.

saints.text: I know now that true charity consists in bearing all our neighbours’ defects—not being surprised at their weakness, but edified at their smallest virtues.
saints.by: Saint Thérèse of Lisieux, Story of a Soul, chapter 9 (tr. T. N. Taylor, 1912)

saints.text: Keep thyself first in peace, and then thou wilt be able to bring others to peace.
saints.by: Thomas à Kempis, The Following of Christ, book II, chapter 3 (tr. Challoner)

how: When someone’s habit irritates you, remember one of your own that irritates others.
Wait a moment before replying to anything that provokes you.
Look for one small virtue in the person who tries you, and notice it.
If you must correct someone, do it calmly, once, and then let it rest.
habits.start: Today, when someone irritates you, wait for one slow breath before you answer.
habits.examine: Whose faults tried my patience today, and how did I respond?
habits.caution: Patience does not mean putting up with abuse, or failing to correct those in your care; correct calmly when it is your duty.
from: Thomas à Kempis, The Following of Christ, book I, chapter 16, and book II, chapter 3
Saint Thérèse of Lisieux, Story of a Soul, chapter 9
Saint Francis de Sales, Introduction to the Devout Life, part III, chapter 8

habits.title: Offering it up
habits.sub: Small sufferings joined to Christ’s
what: Every day brings things we would not choose: a headache, a long wait, tiredness, a disappointment, someone’s coldness. “Offering it up” means giving these to God, joined to Christ’s sufferings, for someone or something in particular. Saint Paul rejoiced in his sufferings because in his flesh he filled up “those things that are wanting of the sufferings of Christ” for the Church.

Christ’s sacrifice lacks nothing; but he lets us share in his work, so that what we suffer in union with him can help others. Saint John Paul II wrote a whole letter on this, Salvifici Doloris. It turns what seems wasted into a gift.

saints.text: If I am in sickness, my sickness may serve him; in perplexity, my perplexity may serve him; if I am in sorrow, my sorrow may serve him.
saints.by: Saint John Henry Newman, Meditations on Christian Doctrine, “Hope in God—Creator”

how: When something hurts or frustrates you, say inwardly: “Lord, I offer you this, with your Cross, for …”, and name someone.
Keep one person or intention in mind for the day, so that your offerings have somewhere to go.
Do not go looking for suffering; offer what comes.
Having offered it, do what you sensibly can to ease it.
habits.start: Choose one person to pray for today, and offer for them the first small discomfort that comes.
habits.examine: What did I suffer today, small or great, and did I give it to God for someone?
habits.caution: Offering a suffering never means refusing treatment, pain relief or help; use them, and offer what remains.
from: Saint John Paul II, Salvifici Doloris (1984)
Saint John Henry Newman, Meditations and Devotions, “Hope in God—Creator”

habits.title: A few minutes of silence
habits.sub: Stillness before God each day
what: Most days are full of noise: voices, music, news, notifications, and the noise inside our own heads. Prayer needs some silence, and so does the soul. Thomas à Kempis writes that in silence and quiet the devout soul goes forward and learns the secrets of the Scriptures.

The habit is simple: a few minutes each day of deliberate quiet before God, without words, without a screen, without trying to achieve anything. It may be in a church, a parked car, a garden or a corner of the kitchen. It also widens into the day: leaving some silences unfilled.

saints.text: In silence and quiet the devout soul goes forward, and learns the secrets of the scriptures.
saints.by: Thomas à Kempis, The Following of Christ, book I, chapter 20 (tr. Challoner)

saints.text: Seek a proper time to retire into thyself, and often think of the benefits of God.
saints.by: Thomas à Kempis, The Following of Christ, book I, chapter 20 (tr. Challoner)

how: Choose a time and place for three to five minutes of quiet each day, and keep it.
Begin by placing yourself before God; then simply stay, letting thoughts pass without following them.
Leave one ordinary stretch of the day unfilled: a journey without music, a walk without earphones.
If you live with others, look for the quiet that is possible, not the quiet you wish you had.
habits.start: Today, sit for three minutes in silence before God, with your phone in another room.
habits.examine: Did I give God any silence today?
habits.caution: If silence brings up distress or dark thoughts, keep it short, pray with a psalm instead, and talk to someone you trust.
from: Thomas à Kempis, The Following of Christ, book I, chapter 20
Saint Francis de Sales, Introduction to the Devout Life, part II, chapter 12

habits.title: Turning from bad thoughts at once
habits.sub: Not arguing with them, not entertaining them
what: Sin usually begins as a thought: a resentment, a lustful image, a proud comparison, a temptation to despair. Thomas à Kempis describes the stages: first a bare thought, then a strong imagination, then delight, and at last consent. The time to resist is at the first knock, when it is easiest.

The saints’ advice is not to argue with such thoughts or examine them, which only gives them room, but to turn at once to God and to something else. Saint Francis de Sales says that small temptations are best simply despised. Thoughts that come against our will are not sins; only consent is.

saints.text: Withstand the beginning, after-remedies come too late.
saints.by: Thomas à Kempis, The Following of Christ, book I, chapter 13 (tr. Challoner)

saints.text: Therefore despise all these trivial onslaughts, and do not even deign to think about them.
saints.by: Saint Francis de Sales, Introduction to the Devout Life, part IV, chapter 9

how: When a bad thought comes, do not debate it; turn your mind to God with a word, such as the name of Jesus.
Then give your mind something else: work, a conversation, a task for your hands.
Do not go back afterwards to check whether you consented; if you turned away, you did well.
Notice what usually sets these thoughts off, and avoid it when you can.
habits.start: Choose a short prayer, such as “Jesus, help me”, to say the moment an unwanted thought appears.
habits.examine: Was there a thought today that I entertained too long, and one I turned from quickly?
habits.caution: Unwanted thoughts that keep returning against your will are not sins; if they are constant and distressing, they may be intrusive thoughts a doctor can help with, and a confessor will usually tell you not to confess them.
from: Thomas à Kempis, The Following of Christ, book I, chapter 13
Saint Francis de Sales, Introduction to the Devout Life, part IV, chapters 3, 7 and 9
Saint Ignatius of Loyola, Spiritual Exercises, general examen, on thoughts

habits.title: Serving someone in person
habits.sub: A work of mercy with your own hands
what: Christ said that whatever we do for the least of his brethren we do for him. Giving money matters, but the saints also served with their own hands: Saint Francis de Sales asks even the well-off to be servants of the poor, to nurse them and visit them in their homes, as Saint Louis of France did.

This habit is to do regularly, in person, one of the works of mercy: visiting someone sick or alone, feeding the hungry, welcoming a stranger, comforting someone who grieves. Saint Thérèse wrote that charity must not remain shut up in the heart. It changes the one who serves as much as the one who is served.

saints.text: Above all I know that charity must not remain shut up in the heart.
saints.by: Saint Thérèse of Lisieux, Story of a Soul, chapter 9 (tr. T. N. Taylor, 1912)

saints.text: Be the servant of the poor: tend them with your own hands, and go to their homes as well as bringing them to yours.
saints.by: Saint Francis de Sales, Introduction to the Devout Life, part III, chapter 15 (our paraphrase)

how: Choose one person near you who is sick, old, lonely or struggling, and visit or call them regularly.
Find a parish or local group that serves the poor in person, and give it a fixed time, even once a month.
When you give, give with a word and a look, not only a coin.
Begin at home: the person who most needs your time may live with you.
habits.start: This week, visit or call one person who is alone, and listen more than you speak.
habits.examine: Whom did I serve today with my own hands or time, and whom did I pass by?
habits.caution: Serve within your state of life: your family’s real needs come first, and you need not take on more than you can carry.
from: Saint Francis de Sales, Introduction to the Devout Life, part III, chapter 15
Saint Thérèse of Lisieux, Story of a Soul, chapter 9
Matthew 25:31 to 46

habits.title: Joy
habits.sub: A glad heart, even on ordinary days
what: Christian joy is not a mood. It rests on what is true whatever the day is like: that God made us, loves us, has redeemed us and is with us. Writing from prison, Saint Paul told the Philippians to rejoice in the Lord always. The saints were often the most cheerful people in the room; Newman says that no one ever saw Saint Philip Neri melancholy.

This habit is to cultivate gladness on purpose: to notice good things, to laugh easily, to bring a light heart to the people around you, and to resist the low sadness that turns in on itself. Against that sadness Saint Francis de Sales recommends prayer, hymns and spiritual songs, and the company of good people.

saints.text: No one ever saw Philip melancholy; those who went to him always found him with a cheerful and smiling countenance, yet mixed with gravity.
saints.by: Saint John Henry Newman, of Saint Philip Neri, Meditations and Devotions (novena of Saint Philip)

saints.text: Our Lord loves the glad of heart, the children that greet him with a smile.
saints.by: Saint Thérèse of Lisieux, Counsels and Reminiscences, in Story of a Soul (tr. T. N. Taylor, 1912)

how: Greet the people you live with as if you were glad to see them.
Sing, hum or listen to sacred music when you feel low.
Notice the good things of the day, enjoy them, and say so.
When sadness turns you in on yourself, do something for someone else.
habits.start: Today, smile at the first person you see, and mean it.
habits.examine: Where did I find joy today, and did I share it?
habits.caution: Joy is not forced cheerfulness: grief and sorrow are not failures, and depression is an illness to be treated, not a lack of joy to blame yourself for.
from: Saint John Henry Newman, Meditations and Devotions, novena of Saint Philip Neri
Saint Thérèse of Lisieux, Counsels and Reminiscences
Saint Francis de Sales, Introduction to the Devout Life, part IV, chapter 12

habits.title: Remembering death calmly
habits.sub: Living today as you would wish to be found
what: The saints thought about death often, not to frighten themselves but to see clearly. Remembering that life is short sorts out what matters from what does not, makes small grudges and ambitions look foolish, and gives each day its weight. “In all thy works remember thy last end,” says Sirach, “and thou shalt never sin.”

The habit is a brief, calm thought, perhaps at night: if this were my last day, would I be at peace with God and with others? It goes together with trust in God’s mercy and with prayer for a good death.

saints.text: How happy and prudent is he who strives to be such now in this life, as he desires to be found at his death.
saints.by: Thomas à Kempis, The Following of Christ, book I, chapter 23 (tr. Challoner)

how: At night, as you lie down, give your life into God’s hands: “Into thy hands, O Lord, I commend my spirit.”
Now and then ask whether there is anything you would want to put right if you died soon; then put it right.
Pray for a good death, for yourself and for those who are dying today.
Keep the thought of death joined to hope: it is the way home.
habits.start: Tonight, before sleep, say: “Into thy hands, O Lord, I commend my spirit.”
habits.examine: Is there anything I would want to put right if this had been my last day, and can I begin tomorrow?
habits.caution: If you are grieving, seriously ill, or troubled by fear or dark thoughts, leave this habit aside for now; it is meant to bring peace, not fear.
from: Thomas à Kempis, The Following of Christ, book I, chapter 23
Saint John Henry Newman, Meditations and Devotions, “Prayer for a Happy Death”

habits.title: Purity of heart
habits.sub: Guarding the heart, and asking help each night
what: “Blessed are the clean of heart: for they shall see God.” Purity of heart includes chastity, but it is more than avoiding sins against it. It is an undivided heart: thoughts, desires and looks that are honest and loving, and that see other people as persons and never as objects. Saint Francis de Sales calls purity the lily among virtues.

It is kept by small daily choices about what we look at, what we dwell on, and the company and media we choose, and above all by prayer. An old and simple custom is to say three Hail Marys before sleep, asking Our Lady for purity of heart and body.

saints.text: Purity is the lily among virtues—by it men approach to the Angels.
saints.by: Saint Francis de Sales, Introduction to the Devout Life, part III, chapter 12

saints.text: Of a truth, my daughter, without purity no one can ever see God.
saints.by: Saint Francis de Sales, Introduction to the Devout Life, part III, chapter 12

how: Turn away at once from images and thoughts that lead to lust, without studying them.
Avoid, where you can, the places, apps and company that you know make it harder.
Each night, say three Hail Marys, asking Our Lady for a pure heart.
If you fall, go to confession and begin again; do not stay away from God out of shame.
habits.start: Tonight, before sleep, say three Hail Marys for purity of heart.
habits.examine: Did I guard my eyes and thoughts today, and did I see others as persons to be loved?
habits.caution: Temptations and unwanted thoughts are not sins; if this area brings you scruples, follow your confessor’s advice and do not examine yourself on it every night.
from: Saint Francis de Sales, Introduction to the Devout Life, part III, chapters 12 and 13
Catechism of the Catholic Church, 2517 to 2520

habits.title: Work done well and finished
habits.sub: Ordinary work as an offering
what: Most of life is work: a job, study, housework, caring for others. “Whatsoever you do,” writes Saint Paul, “do it from the heart, as to the Lord.” Saint Benedict, who joined work to prayer, called idleness the enemy of the soul. Work done carefully, honestly and to the end is itself an offering to God and a service to others.

Saint Francis de Sales adds that we should work with care but without anxiety, taking our duties quietly one after another. The habit is to do the next piece of work properly, to finish what we begin, and to leave the result to God.

saints.text: Accept the duties which come upon you quietly, and try to fulfil them methodically, one after another.
saints.by: Saint Francis de Sales, Introduction to the Devout Life, part III, chapter 10

saints.text: Whenever we are doing well we are always doing enough and doing it sufficiently fast.
saints.by: Carlo Giuseppe Quadrupani, Light and Peace, chapter 14 (tr. 1898)

saints.text: Idleness is the enemy of the soul.
saints.by: Saint Benedict, Rule, chapter 48 (our translation)

how: Offer your work to God when you begin it.
Do one thing at a time, and give it your attention.
Where you can, finish what you have started before taking up something new.
Do the dull parts as carefully as the interesting ones.
habits.start: Today, finish one task you have left half done, carefully, and offer it to God.
habits.examine: Did I work today with care and honesty, and did I finish what I could?
habits.caution: Doing work well is not perfectionism; done and offered is better than perfect and anxious.
from: Saint Francis de Sales, Introduction to the Devout Life, part III, chapter 10
Saint Benedict, Rule, chapter 48
Carlo Giuseppe Quadrupani, Light and Peace, chapter 14 (Herder, 1898)
Saint John Henry Newman, “A Short Road to Perfection”

habits.title: Keeping Sunday
habits.sub: A day of rest, worship and family
what: Sunday is the day of the Resurrection, and the Church asks us to keep it holy: by taking part in Mass, and by resting from the work and business that would keep us from worship, from joy and from the rest of mind and body. The sabbath, the Lord said, was made for man.

Saint John Paul II wrote in Dies Domini that Sunday is both the Lord’s day and our day: a day for God, for unhurried time with family and friends, for joy, and for works of mercy. Keeping it is an inward habit as much as an outward one: once a week, deliberately stepping out of the rush and remembering what it is all for.

saints.text: Saint Louis Martin, the father of Saint Thérèse, would not do business on Sundays, though it cost him customers.
saints.by: As told by Bishop Guy Gaucher (our summary)

saints.text: Sunday is the Lord’s day and also our own: a day of rest and joy, of family and friends, and of charity.
saints.by: Saint John Paul II, Dies Domini (1998) (our summary)

how: Plan the week so that shopping, chores and work messages can wait until Monday where possible.
Make Mass the centre of the day, and read the Gospel beforehand.
Give unhurried time to family or friends: a meal, a walk, a visit.
Do one work of mercy: a visit to someone alone, a call, a kindness.
habits.start: This Sunday, leave one piece of work until Monday, and give that time to someone you love.
habits.examine: How did I keep last Sunday, and what can I do now to make the next one a day for God and for others?
habits.caution: Some must work on Sundays, in care, emergencies and essential services, or because they have no choice; the Church asks rest as far as you can, not guilt.
from: Saint John Paul II, Dies Domini (1998), 52 to 69
Code of Canon Law, canon 1247
Bishop Guy Gaucher, on Louis and Zélie Martin (secondary)

about: Saint Ignatius of Loyola teaches what he calls the particular examen. Instead of trying to improve everything at once, you choose one fault to overcome, or one virtue to grow in, and attend to it for a time. You resolve on it as you rise, look at it again at midday, and at night ask how the day went, comparing one day with the last (Spiritual Exercises, 24 to 31). Saint Francis de Sales gives the same counsel: choose one virtue to aim at, especially the one opposed to the fault that most besets you, without neglecting the others.

Here you can choose one of these habits as your focus for a few weeks. It will appear when you offer the day in the morning and in the midday pause, and the evening examen will ask its question. Ignatius had those making the Exercises mark their falls on a little chart; the app keeps his attention to one thing but leaves out the marks: there is no counting, no score and no streak. When the weeks are over, keep the habit as part of your rule of life, rest for a while, or choose another.
cautions: One thing at a time, small enough to be concrete. Do not change your focus often, and never in a time of desolation: Saint Ignatius’s rule is to keep, in a dark time, the resolutions you made before it.

For a limited time: a few weeks, not for ever. Growth in virtue is God’s work in us before it is ours, and it is slower than we would like; a focus that has become a burden has either done its work or needs to be put down.

Not for the scrupulous without a confessor’s advice. Saint Ignatius wrote his notes on scruples in the same book, and Saint Francis de Sales wants our displeasure at our faults to be quiet, steady and gentle. If a focus makes you anxious, or keeps you checking yourself all day, set it aside and speak to your confessor.

beforePrayer.text: One Our Father said devoutly is worth more than many prayers hurried over.
beforePrayer.by: Saint Francis de Sales, Introduction to the Devout Life, part II, chapter 1

beforePrayer.text: Before you begin, remember that God is everywhere, and very specially present in your own heart.
beforePrayer.by: After Saint Francis de Sales, Introduction to the Devout Life, part II, chapter 2

beforePrayer.text: Before you begin: whom are you about to speak to, and who are you who speak to him? Think of it for a moment, then begin.
beforePrayer.by: After Saint Teresa of Avila, The Way of Perfection, chapter 22

beforePrayer.text: Say the words knowing what they mean and to whom you are saying them; that is what makes a spoken prayer a prayer.
beforePrayer.by: After Saint Teresa of Avila, The Way of Perfection, chapters 24 and 25

beforePrayer.text: You need not think great thoughts. Only look at him, and know that he is looking at you.
beforePrayer.by: After Saint Teresa of Avila, The Way of Perfection, chapter 26

beforePrayer.text: How can you ask to be heard of God, when you yourself do not hear yourself?
beforePrayer.by: Saint Cyprian, On the Lord’s Prayer, 31

beforePrayer.text: Let all carnal and worldly thoughts pass away, nor let the soul at that time think on anything but the object only of its prayer.
beforePrayer.by: Saint Cyprian, On the Lord’s Prayer, 31

beforePrayer.text: Not many words, but a pure heart: let your prayer be short and pure.
God and his angels are here; let your mind keep pace with your voice.
Pray as the old farmer of Ars prayed before the tabernacle: “I look at him, and he looks at me.”
beforePrayer.by: After Saint John Vianney, the Curé of Ars

beforePrayer.text: We need only to recognize God intimately present with us, to address ourselves to him every moment.
beforePrayer.by: Brother Lawrence, The Practice of the Presence of God, fourth conversation

beforePrayer.text: You need not have words. Asked what she said to Jesus, Saint Thérèse answered: “I say nothing—I only love him!”
beforePrayer.by: After Saint Thérèse of Lisieux, Story of a Soul, epilogue
